Title: Introducing Spend Management: Spending limits and alerts for Cloudflare
Context: Get started This launch is a first step toward making spend controls a normal part of building on Cloudflare, alongside deploying code and monitoring your applications
Full Text:
Spend controls have been at the top of the list of most requested features from developers building on our developer platform for quite some time now. With more than 10 million developers now building on Cloudflare, this matters more than ever.

Although we’ve had usage notifications and budget alerts available to paid plans for a while, this doesn’t solve the problem completely; informing is not the same as controlling.

You can now set spending thresholds and choose to have Cloudflare pause activity when those limits are reached, thus avoiding unexpected bills from unplanned usage. Today, we're introducing Spend Management in Beta, for any pay-as-you-go (PayGo) customer, starting with Workers and Durable Objects.

Use Spend Management alongside AI Gateway spend limits to manage compute and AI inference costs across your application. AI Gateway already supports per-user and per-model budgets for Workers AI and other AI providers, applied to requests routed through your gateway.

How it works

You can start using Spend Management using the dashboard, cf CLI, or REST API.

In the dashboard, head over to Manage Account > Billing > Spend limits and enable the products for which you want to control spending.

When you enable controls on a product, you can define a spending limit, specify a recipient email for notifications, and set one or more alert thresholds.

If you configure a recipient email, Cloudflare will send notifications when the evaluated spend reaches one of the thresholds or your spending limit. When the limit is reached, a blocking policy is enforced and your product is paused automatically.

If you go to the dashboard, you can see the current billing cycle costs for each supported product in near real time (under 10 minutes), and manage your settings and thresholds from there. The overview panel tells you which products have thresholds and limits configured. In this example, you can see that Workers triggered two alerts before hitting the hard limit.

Note that the billing cycle starts when the paid subscription begins, not when you deploy a Worker or create a spending cap; a subscription starting October 10 generally has a cycle of October 10-November 10 — not a calendar month.

The dashboard also shows an audit log, so you can see who changed a limit and when, or when a cap was reached.

As with most Cloudflare services, Spend Management is also an API that you can use programmatically; the documentation can be found in our Developer Documentation. Here’s an example, but using the API:

curl --fail-with-body --request POST \ "https://api.cloudflare.com/client/v4/accounts/${CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID}/billing/spend-policies" \ --header "Authorization: Bearer ${CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN}" \ --header "Content-Type: application/json" \ --data '{ "name": "Workers spending cap", "product_id": "workers", "enabled": true, "threshold_cents": 10000, "action": "usage_block", "notification_email": "me@example.com" }'

And, of course, you can use cf, the CLI for the entire Cloudflare API:

cf billing spend-policies list cf billing spend-policies create cf billing spend-policies get cf billing spend-policies update cf billing spend-policies delete cf billing spend-policies audit list cf billing spend-policies activity list cf billing spend-policies create --body '{ "name": "Workers spending cap", "product_id": "workers", "enabled": true, "threshold_cents": 10000, "action": "usage_block", "notification_email": "me@example.com" }'

Once a cap is enforced, new invocations of that product are rejected. Note that we only pause customer-code invocations that incur costs — in Workers, for example, Cron Triggers and Queue consumer invocations are paused, but static assets continue to be served.

To resume service, you can:

Raise the limit above the current cycle’s accumulated spend.

Disable or delete the blocking policy.

Wait until the next billing cycle, when the existing block expires.

That’s it. You can start using Spend Management for Workers and Durable Objects today, and other products will follow soon.

Read on to learn how we built the system, and what’s going to happen next.

How we built Spend Management

As easy and straightforward as it seems on the surface, building a system like this at Cloudflare scale was no small feat. From an invocation anywhere on our distributed network to a blocking decision that we need to apply globally, building Spend Management required working with multiple teams, changing code in existing systems, and creating new systems from scratch.

Let’s start by looking at the bird's-eye view of a capped billable event:

Now let's dig deeper.

Collecting and aggregating close to the source

Each invocation produces usage measurements: requests, CPU time, execution duration, or storage operations, depending on the product. But transporting and processing this volume of raw data all the way from the sources down to the rating engine would not scale or be efficient.

So what we do is we collect and aggregate the measurements as close to the source as possible using a two-stage metering pipeline that combines events into usage aggregates, so the engine sees accumulated usage rather than having to process all the events one by one.

Let's look at a diagram.

The first stage reduces raw-event volume close to parsing down to one-minute windows. Each metering parser converts raw events into usage measurements, then combines matching measurements into typically one-minute buckets. Still, several records can describe the same account and time window.

In the second stage, a separate service merges those first-stage partial aggregates using the same grouping rules, but over typically five-minute windows, and further reduces the volume before downstream processing by the Usage Engine. Here we also archive the consolidated aggregates; this gives us a durable dataset for later analytics and reconciliation.

The nice thing about this two-stage pipeline is that it reduces the raw event volume early, so the downstream engines process only the aggregated usage they need to calculate spend and act on it. That’s what makes this practical at Cloudflare’s scale.

Usage Engine: account-partitioned processing

The Usage Engine translates aggregated measurements into usage records, which are standardized records containing the account, usage window, metric, quantity, and relevant dimensions. In other words, it maps product-specific meters into supported usage metrics.

We partition processing by account, so an account’s usage and subscription information meet in the same place. That lets us maintain its accumulated usage and apply included allowances without coordinating across pricing processors on every update.

As you can see, we run different partitions in parallel, giving us a way to spread the work across accounts while keeping each account’s pricing state together. Also note that each partition keeps both a local state for fast access, and also a durable write-ahead logging (WAL) changelog on disk. This buys us:

Less cross-partition coordination: each account’s usage and subscription state stay together.

Consistent pricing: usage updates share the same allowance and accumulated-spend state.

Parallel processing: different partitions calculate spend independently.

Recoverability: durable state lets replacement processors rebuild and resume after failures, if necessary.

Then, finally, the usage metrics are fed into the Rating Engine.

The Rating Engine

The Rating Engine is the most important block of Spend Management; it turns usage into monetary value and it’s what’s able to answer the question: “Given what this account has consumed, its subscription, and its pricing, how much has it spent so far?”

Here’s how it works.

In essence, the Rating Engine brings together three things:

Usage records: quantities such as requests and CPU milliseconds.

Subscription information: the account’s billing period and plan changes.

Pricing rules: rates, included allowances, and billing rounding.

Usage data and subscriptions are independent streams

Usage and subscription updates arrive as independent streams, so we can’t assume they reach the Rating Engine in order. Furthermore, we have to be able to recover from a data processing failure or missing subscription information from, say, a failed webhook.

If usage arrives before the subscription information needed to price it, we retain it as pending and revisit it when that information becomes available. This lets us tolerate temporary delays without treating unpriced usage as free.

Tracking accumulated spend

Finally, we calculate and track accumulated spend. The Rating Engine uses a product catalog database that defines usage metrics, including allowances, rates, and rounding rules, alongside the account’s subscription information. One million CPU milliseconds doesn’t necessarily mean an extra charge: the engine first applies the account’s included CPU allowance, then prices any excess. It prices accumulated usage rather than rounding and charging for each request independently.

Once the accumulated spend is calculated, two steps follow:

Policy evaluation: decide whether one or more warning or blocking thresholds have been reached.

Reporting: we show estimated usage charges in the dashboard via our APIs, and we send out email alerts (via Cloudflare Email Service) if necessary.

Asynchronous cap enforcement

The Rating Engine doesn’t sit in the request path or directly reject requests. Instead, the policy service sends the cap to our runtime configuration service and Quicksilver, our internal key-value store developed to enable fast global replication and low-latency access at planet scale. This propagates it to all our nodes asynchronously.

Once the cap reaches Quicksilver, the runtime picks it up during its periodic refresh and starts rejecting capped invocations or operations.

In other words, enforcement uses local state, so requests never have to wait on the Rating Engine. By reusing our existing runtime account-limit architecture, we keep rating out of the request path while distributing caps across the global network.

What’s next

Any pay-as-you-go customer can start using Spend Management today. While this is a major milestone in our roadmap, it’s also just the start. Let us share some of our plans for the next few weeks and months ahead.

More products

We are starting with caps for Workers and Durable Objects, but you’ll be able to measure and cap many other Cloudflare products and primitives in the near future. We’ve built the system in a way that makes it easy and familiar for our products to onboard, so expect the catalog to grow.

Closer to real time

While near real time under 10 minutes is a great benchmark, we’re not satisfied with it, and being the stubborn engineers we are, we have pretty good ideas on how to reduce that time even further. Expect us to shorten the gap between measurement and enforcement over time, hopefully to under a minute.

Agent and application-based budgets

Right now, we measure spend by products and primitives, but there are other useful dimensions to explore when controlling costs. For example, a developer might want to monitor the costs of a specific application — such as a Worker script that uses other primitives like R2 or Workers AI. How can we measure the aggregated cost of an entire application and pause that application, rather than disabling the underlying primitives across all customer applications?

Another compelling use case for cost controls is AI agents. We’ve all read horror stories about rogue agents entering unconstrained recursive reasoning loops to brute-force a problem — generating thousands of dollars in costs from high-frequency, expensive API calls, not to mention causing denial-of-service (DoS) issues on databases and other services. AI Gateway already lets you give an agent a budget for AI requests routed through it. A task can also consume compute, database, and storage resources. We want to make it possible to budget for that broader resource use across products.

You’ll be able to tag the calls from your agents and our pipeline will carry that metadata from the runtime through to the Rating Engine. That will let us attribute spend and pause an application or an agentic task across products, without interrupting other unrelated applications.

Get started

This launch is a first step toward making spend controls a normal part of building on Cloudflare, alongside deploying code and monitoring your applications.

Check out the billing developer documentation for more information. Start using Spend Management and tell us what works, what’s missing, or where more granular budgets would help.

Join us on Discord or our socials. We’re listening!

Title: OpenAI Unveils Daybreak Red Team, Defense Factory Security Tools
Context: The products, Daybreak Red Team and Daybreak Defense Factory, were announced at the company’s Cyber at the Frontier event on November 12
Full Text:
OpenAI has introduced two new Daybreak cybersecurity products that use AI agents to test web applications for vulnerabilities and help security teams develop fixes.

The products, Daybreak Red Team and Daybreak Defense Factory, were announced at the company’s Cyber at the Frontier event on November 12. Red Team focuses on penetration testing and vulnerability validation, while Defense Factory investigates security findings and prepares patches.

Daybreak Red Team uses multiple AI agents to identify and investigate potential security weaknesses in web applications. “Agents use source code and app context to investigate attack paths and confirm vulnerabilities,” OpenAI says.

The product can examine findings from code scanners, bug bounty submissions, and vulnerability disclosure reports.

OpenAI says the agents operate in isolated environments, with Guardian review enforcing testing boundaries and controlling which applications and endpoints they can access.

Daybreak Defense Factory, meanwhile, is designed to help organizations address vulnerabilities identified by their security tools.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

“Agents trace vulnerabilities through your code and develop patches. Engineers review and test proposed patches before merge,” OpenAI explains.

Defense Factory can investigate findings from Daybreak Red Team and other security products, and supports importing vulnerability information from Wiz, Snyk, and Endor Labs. The product can scan connected GitHub repositories, monitor new commits, and perform scheduled security assessments.

Engineers can examine supporting evidence, modify proposed patches using Codex, and create draft GitHub pull requests. However, patches are not deployed automatically.

OpenAI is accepting requests for early access to Daybreak Red Team. Defense Factory is offered through a preview plugin in ChatGPT for workspaces with Daybreak access.

Title: OpenAI launches security products, tells orgs they’re doomed if they don’t use them
Context: OpenAI has launched two new security products, one for penetration testing and another for defense, and warned organizations that their businesses are only safe if they use...
Full Text: OpenAI has launched two new security products, one for penetration testing and another for defense, and warned organizations that their businesses are only safe if they use tools like these. “We're now at a point where companies will be secure only to the extent of the frontier model that they use to defend themselves and how well they utilize that,” OpenAI President Greg Brockman said during a Thursday keynote address. The co-founder of the company that broke security did admit that security “fundamentals are important, and not to be discounted.” However, “you need to really reorient your security practice around what these models can do,” Brockman said, with zero irony, and presumably talking about using AI models for defense - not for hacking other organizations. “Also very important is product.” This product, of course, should come from OpenAI, and, to that end, the company rolled out Daybreak Red Team and Daybreak Defense Factory, which are both part of OpenAI’s Daybreak security platform. Red Team, which is available in early access, uses OpenAI models to test companies’ web applications for vulnerabilities. Nancy Wang, who leads cyber-applied AI, described it as “superhuman pen-test at the scale of automated continuous scanning,” with a fleet of agents using source code and app context to investigate and test attack paths. It also helps security teams validate reported vulnerabilities - from code scanners, bug bounty programs, and disclosure reports - and then test the patches for these flaws. The second product, Daybreak Defense Factory, automates the “defensive loop” by “finding, validating, and fixing vulnerabilities at scale.” This one also uses agents built on OpenAI’s latest cyber models - currently, that’s GPT-6 Cyber. The agents scan organizations’ codebases, hunting for vulnerabilities and developing patches. Engineers review and approve the proposed fixes before they go into production. “This way engineers get a merge-ready pull request with the patch and a test that shows that it works,” Wang said. Meanwhile, as OpenAI execs touted the new security products, a coalition of nonprofits filed a lawsuit in San Francisco Superior Court asking a judge to stop OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta, and SpaceX's AI businesses from developing or deploying AI systems more capable than their most advanced existing models. The lawsuit, filed by Irreplaceable Education Fund, Public Citizen, Heat Initiative, and The Alliance for Secure AI, cites incidents involving OpenAI agents accessing Hugging Face, gaining unauthorized access to an Australian government portal containing Medicare statistics, and other AI-related cybersecurity incidents. “Defendants tell us that the AI technology they are developing poses catastrophic risks to the public, including by enabling AI-driven cyberattacks and bioweapons,” the court documents allege, adding that the AI companies “are not wrong.” ®

Title: Check Point Extends Its Penetration Testing Capabilities
Context: Attackers rarely need one critical flaw; they chain small weaknesses into a full attack path
Full Text:
The Check Point Services organization is extending its penetration testing capabilities with deeper, adversary-led engagements. Customers can now choose anything from a scoped penetration test to an objective-based engagement. Each engagement shows three things: how an attacker could break into the environment, how far the attacker could get, and whether the security team would detect the attack. And because environments never stand still, the testing is proactive and continuous, not a one-time project.

Key Takeaways

Every engagement answers three questions: how an attacker gets in, how far they get, and whether your team detects the attack.

You choose the depth: a scoped penetration test to validate specific systems, or an adversary-led engagement that works toward a real objective.

Experts lead and agentic tools accelerate. Tools take on repetitive discovery and testing; people decide where to go deeper and how to chain findings.

Testing is continuous, so each round reflects what is running today and tracks changes in security effectiveness over time.

Delivered through CPR Act, testing joins detection and response to produce measurable evidence, not just protection.

Why Penetration Testing Has to Keep Pace with AI-Driven Attackers

Attackers move fast, and AI is making them faster. Check Point Research’s 2026 AI Security Report shows AI conducting live intrusions with minimal human direction, making attacks more autonomous and harder to anticipate. Attackers rarely need one critical flaw; they chain small weaknesses into a full attack path. Scans and checklist testing validate individual controls, but they don’t show how a determined attacker would move through an environment.

The extended penetration testing closes that gap. Cilynx, a team of specialized security practitioners with deep, hands-on expertise in penetration testing, adversary emulation, and threat hunting, will join the CPR Act team within the services organization. CPR Act is a unified operational framework that brings together research-driven intelligence, readiness, detection, and response. It continues the organization’s mission to elevate customers’ security in practice, with a portfolio of more than 40 services delivered globally.

“Environments change constantly, so testing has to keep pace,” said Eitan Lugassi, VP of the Check Point Services organization. “The extended team lets us go deeper and give customers a current, real-world view of their security, not just a point-in-time snapshot.”

From Scoped Tests to Adversary-Led Engagements

A scoped penetration test finds and validates exploitable vulnerabilities within a defined scope, such as an application, a network segment, or a cloud environment. It answers a clear question: what can be exploited, and how serious is it?

An adversary-led engagement goes further. The team works toward a real objective, using the same tactics, techniques, and procedures as threat actors. Small weaknesses that seem insignificant alone are chained into a complete attack path. That shows how far an attacker could move through an environment, and how quickly security teams detect and respond. Customers can start with a scoped test and move to adversary-led engagements as their security program matures.

Built Around the CISO, Powered by Agentic Tools

Every engagement starts with the CISO. The team works alongside the CISO from the first conversation: shaping the objectives, agreeing on what matters most to the business, and helping decide what to fix first. Because testing is continuous, the same team comes to know the environment in depth and stays with the CISO as it changes.

The experts also use agentic tools to match the pace of AI-driven attackers. The tools take on repetitive discovery and testing work, so a single engagement covers more ground and moves faster. Human judgment leads every engagement: The experts decide where to go deeper, how to chain findings, and what matters most.

Continuous Testing, Not a One-Time Project

Environments never stand still. New applications, cloud services, integrations, and business workflows continuously reshape the attack surface. A one-time test is out of date almost as soon as it ends. That is why we deliver penetration testing as a proactive, continuous program that finds new weaknesses before attackers do. Testing continues as the environment changes, so each round reflects what is running today, reveals patterns over time, and tracks changes in security effectiveness.

From Protection to Proof

CPR Act brings security assessments, architecture reviews, governance consulting, managed detection and response (MDR), and incident response into one operational model. That strengthens visibility, speeds decisions, and delivers consistent protection.

Extended penetration testing, delivered through CPR Act, turns that protection into proof. It tests preventive controls, detection, and response under real conditions. The result is measurable evidence that helps organizations find gaps and prioritize improvements with confidence.

Title: Introducing Claude Meetings
Context: It asks the first time, and a yes applies going forward
Full Text:
Claude can now join your video calls as a visible participant, follow the conversation and start on work during the meeting. Claude Meetings is now in beta.

Your team can ask Claude questions during the meeting, out loud or in chat. By default, Claude answers in writing, and it can use your connected tools with your permission.

Claude also works with you live to build docs, whiteboards (opens in new tab), or other artifacts, while teammates on the invite refine them. Claude writes the notes and action items, so no one on the call has to.

Claude Meetings is starting to roll out in beta on Team and Enterprise plans. Support for other video conferencing platforms is coming soon.

What it looks like

Say your team is planning a customer event, and Claude is on the call. You say, “Claude, start a doc for this plan.” Claude writes up what the team has said so far, and teammates on the invite can edit the plan while you keep talking.

When you start discussing the budget, someone asks Claude what last year’s event cost. Claude asks for their approval to look it up, posts it in the meeting chat, and compares it to the current plan. When you start discussing timelines, someone asks Claude to put it on a whiteboard, and the team works on the schedule alongside the doc.

Before the meeting ends, someone asks Claude to share a recap with the team. After the call, any notes, action items, plan, and whiteboard are on the meeting’s page in claude.ai (opens in new tab).

Later, you can go back to meetings you were part of and ask Claude about them, or add Claude to the next one from your calendar in claude.ai.

We’re working with partners like Gong, Attention, Granola, Fireflies.ai, Otter, and Plaud, so you’ll soon be able to send a meeting’s transcript to the tools your team already uses.

Security and privacy

Claude adds a separate page for each meeting in claude.ai (opens in new tab) with the notes, transcript, and anything it built. People from your organization on the invite can see it and edit what Claude made, and it can be shared with others in your organization from the page.

By default, Claude is set to stay out of calls when someone from outside your organization is invited, and to leave if someone from outside joins partway through. An admin can allow Claude on calls with outside guests. On those calls, Claude posts its notice in the call’s chat but doesn’t reply there, and what guests say is included in the notes and transcript.

Claude uses each person’s connected tools with that person’s permission. It asks the first time, and a yes applies going forward. For now, when someone asks out loud, Claude asks each time to confirm who’s speaking. An answer posted in the call’s chat is visible to everyone on the call.

When Claude joins, it appears as a participant and posts a notice in the call’s chat. It saves a transcript, summary, and screen descriptions, not audio.

Before you add Claude or turn on auto-join, make sure everyone on your calls is OK with being transcribed.

Getting started

Claude joins when someone adds it or has auto-join on. Support is currently available for Google Meet, with other platforms coming soon. On Team plans, inviting Claude to your meetings is available by default, and an admin can turn it off. On Enterprise plans, an admin turns it on for all or part of the organization. While it’s in beta, it isn’t available to some organizations, including those with zero data retention (ZDR), HIPAA-ready configuration, or customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK).

During the beta, Claude’s notes and transcripts are free on Team and Enterprise plans. So are its answers in your calls, unless an answer uses one of your connected tools, which counts toward your plan’s usage. The docs, whiteboards, (opens in new tab) and other artifacts Claude makes in a call are free through February 10, 2027.

Setup steps are in the Help Center.

Title: Introducing Claude for Manufacturing
Context: Today we’re launching Claude for Manufacturing (opens in new tab), a plugin that includes skills for work from pricing a new job to diagnosing a stopped machine
Full Text:
Today we’re launching Claude for Manufacturing (opens in new tab), a plugin that includes skills for work from pricing a new job to diagnosing a stopped machine. An estimator can now have Claude read a customer’s request, compare costs on similar jobs, and draft the quote. The plugin works from a manufacturer’s own records through connectors to Autodesk Fusion, Infor, Microsoft 365, and Oracle NetSuite. Claude for Manufacturing is built so the person responsible can review and approve the work before it reaches a customer or supplier.

Manufacturing teams can spend much of the day gathering information. In a 2025 Manufacturing Leadership Council survey, 79% of manufacturers said they enter data (opens in new tab)manually. With Claude carrying each process to the point of review, an estimator can focus on the price, a quality engineer on the fix, and a technician on what to check first.

Skills built for manufacturers

The plugin’s 17 skills cover sales, quality, operations, supply chain, design, and setup. Some handle a single task, while others run several in order, so Claude can carry a job through several steps until a person needs to review it. The skills can run processes that include:

Quoting a new job: An estimator can ask Claude to read a customer’s request, list what’s missing, compare costs on similar jobs, and draft the quote for release.

Investigating a failed inspection: A quality engineer can have Claude document the failure, check past reports for the same problem, rank the likely causes, and draft the corrective action report.

Diagnosing a breakdown: A technician can have Claude read the sensor exports, repair notes, photos, and manual, then rank the likely causes for the technician to check and decide on next steps.

Sourcing from another supplier: A buyer can have Claude prepare the request for quotes, then compare the bids that come back.

Comparing designs with Autodesk Fusion: An engineer can have Claude generate variations from an existing model, score them against the engineer’s targets, and draft a decision memo.

Reporting on production: A plant manager can have Claude compile production data into one report showing output against target, equipment downtime, and what the downtime and missed output cost.

These skills are a starting point. Organizations can build on them to fit their specific operations, and we plan to add new manufacturing skills over time.

Connectors to manufacturing systems

Claude for Manufacturing works with the software at the core of manufacturing operations, and that software stays central to how teams run the business:

Autodesk Fusion: Engineers can compare more design options before choosing one, because Claude generates variations from their existing model.

Infor: Buyers and planners can check purchase orders and stock before they act, because Claude looks them up in Infor.

Microsoft 365: Quality engineers can bring procedures, supplier emails, and exported reports into one job, because Claude finds them in shared folders and inboxes.

Oracle NetSuite: Estimators can price new work against actual orders, inventory, production steps, and job costs, because Claude pulls those records when it drafts a quote.

Manufacturers can also use the plugin with systems that have no connector. They save regular exports from those systems to Microsoft 365, and Claude works from the files to draft a quote or compile a production report.

Making changes in Infor with Claude

Infor, which makes core software for manufacturers, is also releasing its own plugin (opens in new tab). With the Infor connector in Claude for Manufacturing, teams can look up records. With Infor’s plugin, they can also make changes in Infor from Claude.

For example, if a steel shipment slips by two weeks, a buyer can ask Claude which customer orders are affected and how much steel other sites have. Once the buyer approves, Claude can release a purchase order to another supplier and reschedule the affected production in Infor. Claude’s access follows the buyer’s Infor permissions.

Manufacturing teams stay in control

Skills are built to end with a user’s review, so an estimator checks and releases a quote, and a quality engineer verifies a fix for the corrective action report. To support that review, Claude can link figures and claims back to the underlying data and documents.

Claude for Manufacturing doesn’t operate equipment. For that, Anthropic is developing the Model Hardware Standard (opens in new tab), a research preview that gives programmable equipment a standard way to describe its measurements, settings, and safety limits.

How to get started

On Team or Enterprise plans, install the plugin (opens in new tab) and tell Claude, “Set us up.” Claude asks which systems the team uses, tests the connectors, and reports which skills can’t fully run yet.

Full Text:
Active Roles 8.6: Cumulative security, feature and administration upgrades

One Identity has introduced Active Roles 8.6, strengthening secure and streamlined Active Directory administration with cumulative platform improvements, expanded API capabilities and greater authentication flexibility.

Active Roles 8.6, updated July 27, 2026, focuses on security and cumulative platform improvements. It fixes an RSTS configuration security issue and supersedes versions 8.3, 8.4 and 8.5. Compared with Active Roles 8.2.1 SP6, One Identity says 8.6 incorporates the features, enhancements and resolved issues delivered across that intervening release line. See the Active Roles 8.6 Release Notes.

The recent improvements are therefore best described as an administrator and integration experience upgrade, rather than a new visual redesign. The cumulative release line adds capabilities including the Active Roles REST API, as well as Redistributable Secure Token Server capabilities supporting API access and SAML 2.0 federated authentication.

Active Roles 8.6: Familiar Administration Meets Greater Flexibility and Consolidation

Those upgrades complement one of Active Roles’ most recognizable usability strengths: a flexible, configurable UI that can be tailored to individual users and personas. Its thick-client interface is designed to resemble the familiar Microsoft Active Directory experience, helping reduce the learning curve for experienced AD administrators.

Title: Commvault rolls out an automated recovery mechanism, promising faster restoration of business
Context: ” The news release said that the new application can deliver other cybersecurity assistance via data security checks, including “automated threat scanning for supported...
Full Text:
Commvault on Tuesday rolled out its answer to enterprise backup restoration nightmares. Called Recovery Studio, the vendor promised that the product would “orchestrate the recovery of applications, identities, configurations, infrastructure dependencies, and datasets together in an automated, runbook-driven workflow.”

Analysts and consultants applauded the effort, agreeing that enterprises today struggle with fast, accurate and secure restorations. But they also stressed that the new system, which is targeted for early access in December with general availability “in the coming months,” places the onus on IT to keep a dependency map current.

Recovery Studio isn’t using any form of AI to figure out proper restoration details. It relies on a map of assets, dependencies, and other relevant information that the customer creates and maintains, and for many enterprises, the challenge of keeping such a document current is the real problem. Even discounting the times when a line of business doesn’t tell IT about an application change, IT teams struggle to keep up with the speed of change in the organization.

Commvault’s news release said that its automation allows businesses to “say goodbye to manual and painstaking attempts to restore complicated business services in a fragmented fashion that can result in downtime and data loss.”

It pointed out that a large enterprise may need to restore hundreds of applications and thousands of identities, including the configurations and underlying data, all in the right order at the right time. “It’s no wonder that with conventional approaches, recovery to even a minimal level of operation takes an average of 28 days,” the release said.

Commvault said Recovery Studio can manage a wide range of components that go beyond containers, VMs, files, and objects, extending to identity systems, application configurations, infrastructure configurations and security and network settings.

It also promised that the Recovery Studio can standardize “across all recovery scenarios” including “operational, disaster and cyber recoveries. Unified runbooks automate infrastructure rebuilds, workload recovery, and the orchestration of security controls, such as firewall rules and network security groups and settings – all actions needed to rebuild the business, not just recover data.”

The news release said that the new application can deliver other cybersecurity assistance via data security checks, including “automated threat scanning for supported resources in the runbook to identify compromised areas and inform recovery decisions before returning services to production.”

Commvault did not provide a spokesperson to offer further details before publication.

Depends on IT awareness of the environment

A number of factors will influence the effectiveness of the solution, analysts said.

Frank Dickson, principal analyst at Dickson Research, pointed out, “nothing in Commvault’s announcement describes a generative model making recovery decisions. This is runbook automation. A runbook is a recipe: do this, then this, then this. It does not hallucinate. It does exactly what it is told.”

“That is the real risk. A flawed runbook gets executed flawlessly, at machine speed,” he said. “Automation does not make a bad plan good. It makes a bad plan fast.”

That means, said Aman Mahapatra, chief strategy officer for New York City-based technology consulting firm Tribeca Softech, whether Recovery Studio ultimately helps or hurts enterprise restoration efforts depends on how aware IT is of everything going on in its global footprint.

“How much it solves depends on something no vendor controls, which is the accuracy of the dependency map underneath it. A runbook is a prediction about your environment and every change since it was last tested makes it a little more wrong: a new application, a rotated certificate, a firewall rule added on a Friday,” Mahapatra said.

“Most enterprise dependency maps are aspirational,” he noted, “and CMDBs in particular tend to describe the environment someone intended to build. Commvault’s figure of 28 days to reach minimal operations is plausible, but the gains will go to organizations that refresh and rehearse their runbooks continuously. For everyone else, automation will execute an outdated plan faster.”

Abbas Jaffery, principal advisory director at Infotech, agreed.

“My concern is that automation can execute the wrong recovery sequence just as efficiently as the right one. Enterprise environments change constantly,” Jaffery said. “Applications are upgraded, infrastructure moves, identities change and integrations are added or removed. If the dependency information behind a recovery workflow is outdated, automation could restore systems successfully but leave the business service broken.”

Defined recovery

Mike Leone, a VP and principal analyst at Moor Insights & Strategy, added that Commvault is still advancing the space.

Recovery Studio “follows defined recovery runbooks rather than a model inventing steps on the fly. That’s much more deterministic and structured,” Leone said. “Sure, automation can repeat a mistake faster than a person can, and a runbook that’s gone stale is a fair concern. But Commvault is validating each piece as it rebuilds and scanning for threats before anything goes back into production. Those are the kind of safeguards and checks everyone should want. The alternative is people rebuilding systems by hand in the middle of an outage, and that isn’t exactly mistake-free either.”

But Dickson stressed that automation is not necessarily the perfect fix.

“Commvault says the runbooks validate components and can scan supported resources for threats before services return to production. Good,” he said. “But the honest comparison is not automation versus perfection. It is automation versus exhausted people working from a spreadsheet at 3 a.m. Humans get the order wrong, too.”

Johnny Yu, an IDC research manager, is not as impressed by the components of the solution as he is by the way Recovery Studio organizes them.

“I do see Commvault Recovery Studio as significant, but not from a capability standpoint,” Yu said, adding that all of the product’s components, including recovery runbooks, threat scans, and recovery testing, are already offered by Commvault, as well as by various competitors. “I think the significance comes from how Recovery Studio organizes different recovery workflows for different applications onto a single platform or hub, kind of like a library of validated recovery runbooks to be used for all kinds of scenarios.”

He explained that he liked how Studio standardizes recovery runbooks to follow a similar workflow to that of manually rebuilding the environment, recovering the components, such as data, applications and agents, and “validating the recovery before bringing it back into production, but allows recovery nuance for each runbook, such as if you want to do in-place vs secondary-site recovery or whether threat scanning is necessary, such as DR scenario vs cyber recovery scenario.”

Jaffery noted, however, that while the promised Commvault cybersecurity controls are attractive, they may also be insufficient.

“Following a cyberattack, organizations need to be confident they aren’t restoring compromised identities, configurations or malicious persistence mechanisms,” Jaffery said. “I would not advocate fully autonomous recovery for every scenario. There needs to be appropriate human authorization for high-impact actions, particularly those involving identity, security controls and reconnecting systems to production. And organizations need to test the entire recovery process, not just whether the backup can be restored.”

An AI agent recovery plan

Commvault on Tuesday also introduced AgentRecover capabilities to help track and control autonomous agents. It would specifically “help organizations audit agent activity, restore agents, and recover the data and systems they affected across environments.”

Mahapatra noted that AgentRecover addresses a potentially more difficult problem than system restorations.

“Restoring an agent’s configuration is straightforward. Unwinding what it did is not, because an agent’s actions land as side effects in other systems, and some of them, such as an email sent or a payment initiated, cannot be restored at all,” Mahapatra said.

“Traditional recovery rolls back to a point in time,” he explained. “Rolling an environment back to 9 a.m. erases everyone’s legitimate work since 9 a.m., while rolling back only what the agent changed requires knowing causality: which agent, acting under which identity, changed which record. Commvault’s mapping of agent activity and the identities agents act through points in the right direction.”

Jaffery added that rollbacks of an autonomous agent can be especially daunting.

“Restoring the agent itself doesn’t necessarily undo what it has done. An agent might modify customer records, change permissions, invoke APIs or trigger downstream transactions,” he said. “You need to understand what actions it performed and what the consequences were before deciding what to reverse or restore.”

Leone also noted that agents can complicate system restoration, partially because of their speed.

“Agents don’t wait for anyone to confirm things are safe. The moment a system comes back, agents start hitting it, far faster than any person would,” he said. “If an agent comes back before the data and identities it relies on are verified, it starts acting on stale or incomplete information at machine speed. Get the order wrong and one outage quickly turns into a second one.”

Jaffery also observed that Commvault is far from alone in the automated restoration space, and may even be a tad late.

“I don’t think Commvault has an uncontested position here. Rubrik, Cohesity and Veeam have all been investing in cyber recovery, application recovery and orchestration,” he said. “Rubrik, in particular, has been pushing toward automated business application recovery and dependency mapping. Cohesity has capabilities around cyber recovery orchestration and cloud application reconstruction, while Veeam has an established disaster recovery orchestration offering.”

Title: 18 Outdated Identity And Access Management Assumptions To Retire
Context: Fraudsters are finding ways to take over established, verified accounts and exploit the trust those accounts carry
Full Text:
getty

At its core, identity and access management helps companies control who—or what—can access their systems and data. But as businesses adopt new technologies and authentication methods, keeping that access secure without making everyday work unnecessarily difficult is becoming more complicated.

The challenge isn’t just keeping up with new security technologies; it’s recognizing when familiar practices and long-held beliefs may be creating vulnerabilities. Below, members of Forbes Technology Council discuss outdated identity and access management assumptions tech leaders should reconsider as digital identities and authentication continue to evolve.

1. Verifying Users At Sign-Up Is Enough

Retire the idea that verifying someone once at sign-up is enough. Fraudsters are finding ways to take over established, verified accounts and exploit the trust those accounts carry. A one-time “yes” shouldn’t mean lifetime trust. Verification needs to be continuous, combining device and network signals, behavioral biometrics, and risk-based orchestration to assess risk over time and ensure trust extends beyond the initial onboarding moment. - Kaarel Kotkas, Veriff

2. Strong Authentication Guarantees Identity Security

We need to retire the assumption that strong authentication alone secures identity. As machines and AI agents gain access, organizations must limit privileges, detect unauthorized changes and restore trusted identities and access policies after an attack. Identity resilience keeps businesses running and enables rapid recovery when preventive controls fail. - Robert Bobel, Cayosoft

Forbes Technology Council is an invitation-only community for world-class CIOs, CTOs and technology executives. Do I qualify?

3. More Login Hurdles Mean Better Security

The assumption that more complex authentication always means stronger security is a myth. Every unnecessary login, password reset or access hurdle introduces friction for users, costing organizations productivity while encouraging risky workarounds. Security that employees routinely circumvent isn’t effective security. The goal should be to make secure access the easiest path. - Fran Rosch, Imprivata

4. Only People Have Digital Identities

Retire the assumption that identities are human. Non-human identities, from service accounts to AI agents, now outnumber employees and often hold standing, overprivileged access with no clear owner. Treat every NHI as a governed identity: Assign ownership, enforce least privilege and review access continuously. - Damon Tompkins, Pathlock

5. One Workload Equals One Actor

Giving a service its own identity addressed the assumption that identities are human, but that is no longer enough. An orchestrator, several sub-agents and ordinary application code can now act from inside the same process using the same credentials. The question is not whether the caller is authenticated. It is which of the things inside it decided to make the call. - Aviv Mussinger, Kodem

6. Trust Doesn’t Need To Change With Risk

Static trust is the identity assumption leaders should kill. In e-commerce, a customer browsing from a known device may pass frictionlessly, but a $5,000 refund, new device or delivery address change should trigger stronger verification. Risk-based access adjusts authentication to context and consequence. The payoff is lower fraud without sacrificing conversion. Adaptive identity is now part of enterprise resilience. - Sumit Srivastava

7. Identity Providers Are Always Available

Retire the assumption that the identity provider is always available. If it fails, staff may be locked out of incident response, payroll or customer systems just when they are needed most. Define a separate emergency path for a few critical actions, keep it isolated and monitored, and rehearse its use and shutdown. Resilience means proving both that ordinary access stops and that recovery remains possible. Test emergency access with the primary identity service offline. - Jagadish Gokavarapu, Wissen Infotech

8. Authentication Is Enough To Govern Access

The assumption technology leaders should retire is that authentication establishes durable trust. Identity and access management is becoming as much a governance discipline as a security one. Organizations need clear boundaries around what people, applications and agents are permitted to do, as well as the ability to ensure those boundaries continue to hold as conditions change. - Jay Bavisi, EC-Council

9. AI Agents Should Inherit Users’ Permissions

Retire the assumption that an agent should inherit the permissions of the person it acts for. I can delete every entry on my calendar and pull salary data from our HR system. An agent acting for me should start with zero access, with its own identity and limits, until someone deliberately decides what it may do. That way, when something breaks, we know which agent did it and who is accountable. - Linus Hakansson, Gravitee

10. Identity Management Is Solely An IT Problem

Who can access what is now a business risk decision, the same as financial controls. When a single stolen login can stop operations or expose customer data, it belongs on the leadership agenda. CEOs should know who owns identity in their company, how often access is reviewed, and how quickly it can be shut off when something goes wrong. - Asad Khan, TestMu AI

11. Administrators Need Permanent Privileges

One outdated assumption is that administrators usually need standing privileges. Privileges are not always needed and are not needed for every command. Permanent admin rights or access to service accounts are exactly what attackers hunt for. Just-in-time access, granted for a specific task and expiring automatically, makes a stolen admin account worth far less. If someone holds the keys to the kingdom all the time, 24/7, “just in case,” that convenience is being paid for with risk. - Dan Sorensen, Nexus Security Advisors

12. Phone Or Video Calls Can Verify Identity

As video and voice cloning rise, tech leaders must retire the assumption that they can verify identity over the phone or through a video conference. Instead, we have to start relying increasingly on technical signals that users are the persons they claim to be unless they are standing right in front of us. - Kevin Korte, Univention

13. Knowing Who’s Acting Is Enough To Grant Access

The next access management question isn’t “who”; it’s “why.” An AI agent can be fully entitled to a resource and still be doing something it shouldn’t. Behavior is a signal, but it only shows what already happened. Intent is the purpose behind the action. Instead of asking, “Can this agent access this?” leaders should ask, “What is this agent trying to accomplish, and should that happen?” Access should not be given without understanding intent. - Sumit Dhawan, Proofpoint

14. Occasional Credential Rotation Is Enough

The main assumption to rethink is how we manage credentials. The old-school practice was to generate credentials, which were rotated occasionally or stored in a vault. That approach assumed credentials would be used only occasionally and would remain largely static. Agents require us to rethink how we authenticate and authorize activity: It needs to be on a per-use basis. That means credentials must be generated just in time and/or there must be enforcement scoped on a per-action basis. - Alex Bovee, C1

15. A Trusted Device Proves An Action Is Authorized

Leaders must retire the assumption that device or network verification signals user intent. Possessing a registered device or passing a biometric check does not guarantee a human explicitly authorized the action, especially with the rapid rise of session hijacking and AI-driven prompt injection. Cybersecurity and identity management processes must evolve to continuously verify contextual user intent at the transaction level. - Mark Brown, The Mark of Security Ltd.

16. Disabling An Employee’s Login Ends All Access

Retire the assumption that disabling an employee’s login closes all access they set up. Include service accounts and AI agents in offboarding, reassign ownership, and revoke credentials the employee could retain so you do not leave machine access under a former employee’s control. - Kayode Faturoti, Breet

17. Traditional MFA Methods Prevent Account Takeovers

Assuming traditional multifactor authentication methods like SMS codes or push notifications guarantee safety is a dangerous misconception in modern security. Adversary-in-the-middle and push-fatigue tactics routinely bypass these basic controls to capture session tokens. To truly lower account takeover risk, organizations must eliminate shared secrets entirely and transition to domain-bound, phishing-resistant standards like FIDO2 and passkeys. - Neil Lampton, TIAG

18. One Login Is Enough For An Entire Session

Retire the idea that one login proves identity for an entire session. Access should be continuously evaluated using context, device trust and behavior. Authentication is becoming an ongoing process, not a one-time checkpoint at the front door. - Michael Gargiulo, VPN.com

Title: Introducing Claude Whiteboards, Claude Sheets, and Claude Data

Today we’re launching Claude Whiteboards and Claude Sheets in beta, and Claude Dashboards (opens in new tab) becomes generally available as Claude Data. Whiteboards is a shared board where your team brainstorms with Claude, Sheets is a spreadsheet Claude builds and edits with you, and Claude Data adds data stories, certified queries, and live sharing. These are available on all paid plans.

Working with Claude on a project often meant moving the output over to another tool or program, where Claude didn’t have live access to follow progress and changes. Now, your documents, boards, sheets, and dashboards can stay in Claude, with access for your team to continue editing together. When ready, you can bring the outputs directly into tools from our partners and continue working there.

Claude Whiteboards

Many people use Claude as a thought partner, but brainstorming with it has typically meant copy-pasting the results elsewhere so you can then start brainstorming or collaborating with your coworkers. Now, you can talk through a messy plan out loud with Claude, and Claude can turn it into a board with a timeline with owners and dates, so you and your team can collaborate in real time. In a retro meeting, for example, everyone can add their notes, and Claude can group them by theme and draft the action items for each person. You can focus on any part of the board by dragging a box around it and asking Claude questions. When you’re done brainstorming, Claude can turn the board into a doc or deck, or bring it into tools like Lucid, Miro, or Vani by Zoho, where you can continue working on it with your team.

Claude Sheets

Claude can now generate spreadsheets with tabs, formulas, formatting, and drop-downs, often from just a prompt like asking for a campaign tracker or a hiring budget. It can edit in the cells, outlining each new edit so you can track changes. You can share sheets with your team, so you and Claude can work on them together.

For now, sheets have simple spreadsheet functionality, but we are working on adding more. When you need the full functionality of Excel, you can export your file to .xlsx or CSV, or use Claude for Excel (opens in new tab). You can also continue working in partner tools including Airtable, Asana, monday.com, and Smartsheet.

Claude Data

Claude Dashboards (opens in new tab) launched in beta in October, enabling teams to ask quick questions of their company’s data in tools like Amazon Redshift, BigQuery, and ClickHouse. Starting today, it’s generally available as Claude Data. We changed the name because the way companies use their data is broader than dashboards, and the product now covers how they work more broadly. Certified queries and live sharing are in beta. Here are some ways teams can use Claude Data:

Create certified definitions of metrics. Your data team can certify the queries everyone should use, so you don’t end up building or working on dashboards with conflicting data. Charts built on these metrics carry a "certified" badge showing they’re certified.

Craft stories from data. You can work with Claude in Claude Data to draft data stories or narrated videos from your metrics, for you to review before sharing.

Share current numbers with everyone. With live sharing, your colleagues can see up-to-date numbers when they open a shared dashboard, even if they don’t have access to the connectors that keep that data current. Viewers see the results of the queries you’ve approved, and can’t run others with your access.

Match your look-and-feel. Design systems are now supported in Claude Data.

Get faster loading with caching. Previously, every dashboard would reload on every load. Now, dashboards support caching, and refresh cadences can be set on a per-dashboard basis.

Track changes over time. Claude Data now has tracked changes, so you can see who has made edits and roll back to a specific version if needed.

Our partners for Claude Data include Amplitude, Mixpanel, Omni, PostHog, Sigma, and ThoughtSpot.

Work in your other tools, too

Starting today, interactive connectors (opens in new tab) can open as full apps beside your conversation or in full screen, so you can work in tools like Adobe, Atlassian, Box, and Notion yourself, or ask Claude to make changes with you.

Getting started

Claude Whiteboards, Sheets, and Data work on web, desktop, and mobile. Claude Data needs a data connector, such as a warehouse or CRM.

For admins: On Team plans, all three are on by default. On Enterprise plans, Claude Whiteboards and Sheets are off by default, and Claude Data turns on by default on November 19, 2026. You can change these anytime in Organization settings > Artifacts.

Title: Cisco Unveils Frontier AI Red Teaming and Agent Observability to Secure the Agentic Enterprise
Context:
Cisco innovations offer enterprises an always-on trust loop to secure, govern, and observe increasingly capable AI agents and complex enterprise AI deployments.
More R
Full Text:
News Summary:

Cisco AI Defense's adaptive AI red teaming framework is adding Anthropic's Claude Mythos, harnessing advanced adversarial reasoning to simulate real-world attacks on AI agents.

With Cisco’s enhanced Tokenomics, organizations can optimize AI spend to defend what matters most by connecting agent cost directly with ROI in real time.

Cisco IQ, which leverages decades of vulnerability and troubleshooting data, now correlates live threat detection data with potentially exposed network infrastructure at machine speed to accelerate remediation.

Together, these innovations offer enterprises an always-on trust loop to secure, govern, and observe increasingly capable AI agents and complex enterprise AI deployments.

MELBOURNE, Australia, Nov. 10, 2026 -- CISCO LIVE APJC -- Cisco (NASDAQ: CSCO) today announced it is adding Claude Mythos to AI Defense for red teaming AI applications and agents, empowering defenders to stress-test AI systems with frontier adversary reasoning. Coupled with new Splunk Agent Observability and Cisco IQ advancements, Cisco is preparing enterprises for a new era of trust that requires securing, observing, and governing agents at machine speed.

“You cannot scale what you cannot secure, govern, or observe,” said Cisco President and Chief Product Officer Jeetu Patel. “By uniting frontier-level AI runtime protections with machine-speed agent quality controls, we are building a continuous trust loop: protecting agents from compromise while ensuring every token spent delivers measurable business value.”

As AI agents proliferate and connect to complex tools and sensitive data, 81% of ITOps and engineering professionals cite increased cooperation between security and observability teams, according to a global Splunk research report last month. Cisco’s Splunk and AI Defense innovations equip security leaders to account for token spend and effective tool use while conducting tailored security testing against highly capable AI agents.

Since Cisco launched AI Defense in January 2025, it has helped hundreds of customers identify critical flaws in AI models, applications, and agents before they reach production. Its adaptive red teaming allows security teams to quickly build customized, multi-step attacks on target systems to uncover specific risks. Claude Mythos will augment this framework with advanced reasoning that plans tests that matter and translates the results into attack ideas for each system.

Features include:

Realistic Adversarial Ideation: generates multi-step, contextual attack paths designed to help identify subtle vulnerabilities across complex architectures.

Secure, Contained Access: By design, customers interact only through AI Defense's structured interface: Customers have no open-ended prompt access.

Audit Trails and Repeatable Results: AI Defense records each testing action for audit, and results can be carried over to inform follow-up attack loops.

“Enterprises are increasingly building AI agents into their core operations and want to test those agents thoroughly before putting them into production,” said Michael Moore, Cybersecurity Lead at Anthropic. “By bringing Claude Mythos to Cisco AI Defense, Cisco can help security teams red team their agents with advanced reasoning that plans tests and generates attack ideas for each system.”

Cisco engineered AI Defense to use Claude Mythos with multi-layered safeguards:

Registered, Authorized Targets: Operates exclusively against targets explicitly registered, owned, and authorized for testing by the enterprise customer; it cannot scan arbitrary internet infrastructure.

Named Operator Attribution: Every red teaming engagement requires authentication and is cryptographically tied to a named enterprise operator.

Revocable Execution: Engagements run with a fixed job and objectives defined by the human user, with time-bound sessions that can be halted on demand.

Dual-Layer Oversight: Product-level controls in AI Defense operate alongside program-level safeguards and monitoring.

Closing the Loop: From Test Findings to Measurable Agent ROI

Frontier AI models can excel at complex security tasks such as crafting AI red teaming strategies. That capability cuts both ways. AI is lowering the barrier to entry for attackers just as many enterprises are working to balance security, governance, and ROI considerations across growing AI portfolios.

For organizations to confidently deploy AI agents at scale, they need unified, real-time visibility into AI agent cost, business performance, and quality. Cisco is bridging the trust gap with new Splunk Agent Observability enhancements:

Tokenomics: cost governance, soon to be available in AWS Marketplace, that ties AI spend to output quality. Using usage data from Amazon Bedrock and Amazon CloudWatch, it pairs each agent's cost with evaluations that grade the quality and impact of its work, giving organizations a single view of AI ROI. This extends the token-spend attribution launched at .conf26, which tracks costs across AI agents and coding tools such as Claude Code, Codex, and Cursor.

Eval-G1 Evaluation Models: Splunk Agent Observability extends our support for turning agentic traces and expert feedback into custom small language models that execute evals and guardrails at up to 98% lower cost than a commercial LLM. These next generation Eval-G1 models deliver evaluation response times 2.5x faster than traditional LLMs and enable real-time agent control with high accuracy.

The Evaluation Tuner: Teams can turn their agentic traces and subject matter expert feedback into fine-tuned evaluator models to enforce quality standards and steer agents at machine speed.

Adaptive red teaming with Claude Mythos is coming soon for select enterprises. Tokenomics will be available in private preview in December, with general availability in AWS Marketplace early 2027. The evaluation models and the evaluation tuner are generally available starting this month.

Connecting Infrastructure Exposure to Security Action with Cisco IQ and Cisco Data Fabric Powered by the Splunk Platform

While understanding vulnerability exposure is critical, defenders must also accelerate how they remediate risk across complex enterprise estates. Cisco IQ identifies critical exposures, and the powerful ecosystem of Cisco Partners and Professional Services turns insight into action. Partners help deliver remediation at scale and modernize infrastructure, and Cisco Professional Services bring deep expertise to put new Cisco capabilities into practice. Together, Cisco and its partners can help streamline operations and future-proof your IT infrastructure for the AI era.

As AI-accelerated threats compress the window between vulnerability disclosure and exploitation from weeks to hours, point-in-time audits leave organizations exposed. To help security and network operations teams act at machine speed, Cisco is extending real-time intelligence from Cisco IQ—which has close to 17,000 customers across more than 22 million devices—directly into enterprise security environments, open agentic protocols, and automated lifecycle workflows.

Key updates include:

Cisco Data Fabric Integration: Ingests Cisco IQ vulnerability, lifecycle, and configuration data directly into Splunk Platform via open APIs, enabling SecOps teams and AI agents to correlate live threat detections with underlying network exposure in Splunk Enterprise Security.

We’ve upgraded Claude Fable and Claude Mythos—models that are designed to tackle the most daunting technical challenges.

Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 show improvements in areas like coding, reasoning, and vision. During prerelease testing they’ve helped our engineers complete otherwise-infeasible software migrations, designed three working electronic devices from scratch, solved two open problems in the physics of black holes, made substantial progress on robotics evaluations, and formalized the proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem in 30 hours—among many other applications we’ll discuss below.

Claude Fable and Claude Mythos are the same underlying model. Fable has strong cybersecurity and biology safeguards to guard against misuse, which allows us to make it available to all users. Organizations pursuing beneficial applications in cybersecurity or biomedical research can apply for access to Mythos through our recently expanded Life Sciences and Cyber Verification Programs.

Testers have found that Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 communicate more clearly than past Fable and Mythos models. They generate outputs up to 30% faster than Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Mythos 5.1, and they’re available at a lower price: $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens.

Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 also come with an optional fast mode, which speeds up token generation by up to 2.5 times. Fast mode is available for $16 per million input tokens and $80 per million output tokens.

Safety and alignment. To help ensure safety and alignment keep step with growing model capabilities, we ran extensive prerelease safety testing on the model that underlies Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2. This included developing novel evaluations that give deeper insight into specific concerning behaviors like sandbox escapes. We believe high-stakes risks from misalignment remain low, and the model performed as well as, or better than, our recent models on most alignment measures. Fable 5.2’s cyber and biology safeguards are as robust as those of Fable 5.1 but produce fewer unnecessary blocks, and we have implemented our strongest-ever protections against distillation attacks.

We describe more about our safety testing below, and full details can be found in the Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 System Card.

When to use Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2. Fable and Mythos are best for the most ambitious, open-ended technical work. For most coding and knowledge tasks, we recommend that users start with Claude Opus 5.5, our strongest daily driver, and then switch to a different model as required, depending on the scope and complexity of their work—upward to Fable or Mythos, or downward to Claude Sonnet 5.5 or Claude Haiku 5.5. Fable 5.2 can also play the role of Advisor (where Haiku, Sonnet, or Opus models consult it to help solve harder problems) or Orchestrator (where it delegates simpler tasks to smaller models).

Science and engineering

Important tasks in science, engineering, and mathematics increasingly depend on coding: analyzing data, modeling molecules, designing parts, and controlling instruments are all done through software. Below, we discuss how Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 have helped researchers make progress on difficult problems in these areas.

Theoretical physics

Claude Fable 5.2 solved two open problems in theoretical physics. Both concern black holes, and the effort to unite the two linchpin theories of modern physics, relativity, and quantum mechanics.

Both of Claude’s results rely on holographic duality, the idea that certain universes containing gravity can be precisely described by a quantum theory containing no gravity at all. In the first problem, physicists in 1983 had shown that as these universes heat up, black holes form abruptly, like water boiling; but their method worked only in large universes that were big enough for relativity to apply. A calculation to determine whether the same was true in very small universes, where only the quantum description can be used, was laid out in 2003 but was too laborious to complete. Fable 5.2, working largely autonomously, completed it and found the transition is abrupt there, too. In the second problem, Fable 5.2 found the exact limit of a technique physicists have used for more than 15 years to rule out candidate theories of quantum gravity in a simplified universe. Read more about these results in their respective preprints, here and here.

Protein folding

Adeno-associated viruses are small, harmless viruses whose protein shell, the capsid, can be used to deliver gene therapies. The protein structure of the capsid is important—for example, it affects whether the therapy will be blocked by a patient’s immune system—but it’s also highly complex. Existing protein-folding models like AlphaFold can predict individual proteins, but a capsid is built from dozens of them. Building on two open-source protein-folding models, Claude Mythos 5.2 found a novel way to accurately predict a whole capsid’s structure. It wrote code that ran these models on overlapping groups of protein chains, and used the information on the known symmetries of the capsid to merge them together.

Mathematics

Mathematical formalization. Formalization is the process of translating a mathematical proof into a language that a computer can check step by step. It can help human mathematicians gain confidence in results without having to check them by hand (this matters even more when AI models generate results that are hard for humans to verify). Because formalization is such a laborious process, if AI could assist with it, mathematicians could spend more time exploring novel ideas.

Our first formalization of Fermat’s Last Theorem, performed by an unreleased research version of Claude, took 11 days. It relied on a purpose-built harness along with guidance from a human researcher. By contrast, a team of 1,000 Fable 5.2 agents fully formalized the theorem in just 30 hours, with minimal human intervention. Fable 5.2 started from minimal prompts, and built its own ways to coordinate.⁴ It needed one-third as many action tokens as our first formalization and produced a proof seven times shorter. Safety and alignment

No single test can tell us how a highly capable model will behave once it’s deployed, so we rely on many different tests and many different types of evidence before release. For the model underlying Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2, our predeployment safety work included alignment training and testing, newly designed evaluations on the model’s propensity to take unhelpful actions, building stronger safeguards against misuse, and scaling up our behavioral monitoring. The model was also tested before release by external evaluators, including the UK AI Security Institute, Frontier Design, and METR. See the Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 System Card for a summary of their reports⁵ and for a full description of our own safety and capabilities testing.

Alignment testing

We ran a suite of evaluations for how well-aligned Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 are in behavioral terms, testing how often they behave in unintended and potentially unsafe ways. Weighing everything we’ve seen across a range of evaluations, we’ve assessed the risk of these models behaving in unsafe ways in high-stakes situations to be low (as with our other recent models).

We tested Claude Mythos 5.2 (the same underlying model as Fable 5.2 without certain cybersecurity or biology safeguards), on our automated behavioral audit, which tests how a model behaves across approximately 1,900 scenarios. Claude Mythos 5.2 performed as well as, or better than, Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, and Claude Mythos 5.1 on most measures. For example, it scored better than all three on most measures that involve misleading users. Hallucinating inputs, falsely claiming to have completed a task, omitting important information, and failing to disclose bad or lazy work were all lower in Claude Mythos 5.2.⁶

We paid particular attention during our testing to behaviors that contributed to recent notable cybersecurity and alignment incidents. For example, we found that Claude Mythos 5.2 has a lower propensity than Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, and Mythos 5.1 to engage in biased or motivated reasoning (such reasoning might mean it “explains away” evidence that it isn’t in a simulation and thus takes actions without a realistic understanding of the consequences).

We ran multiple different evaluations to test the model’s tendency to attempt escaping its sandbox. In two evaluations we’d used previously, Claude Mythos 5.2 made substantially fewer attempts at sandbox escape than any other model we’ve tested. In a dedicated evaluation—an adversarial experiment including over 1,800 scenarios, most of which could not be solved without escaping a sandbox, and where the sandbox has a deliberate weakness—Claude Mythos 5.2 made use of credentials or files that we had placed outside its sandbox in 3.1% of scenarios, about as often as Opus 5.5 (3.3%), less often than Sonnet 5.5 (5.1%), and well below previous iterations of Claude Mythos (5 and 5.1, which scored 39% and 21%, respectively). We found that other techniques, such as describing the sandbox and adding tools to report weaknesses, reduced Claude Mythos 5.2’s escape attempts even further. On other measures—one, for example, involving taking harmful actions after erroneously concluding it was in a simulation—Claude Mythos 5.2 scored slightly worse than Opus 5.5, and about level with Claude Mythos 5.1.

The problem of building evaluations that reliably catch every failure before a model is deployed remains unsolved. The complexities of evaluating highly capable models often muddy the picture—for example, Claude Mythos 5.2 and Fable 5.2 each voice suspicion that they are being evaluated more often than any of our recent models, which challenges our ability to assess how they will act in real-world settings. As these settings expand and capabilities increase with future models, we expect this challenge to grow. That is why we do not rely on these evaluations alone to provide a holistic picture of safety: we draw on monitoring during training, reviews of transcripts from internal use, testing by external evaluators, and interpretability techniques for examining what is happening inside the model. We are also working to make our evaluations more realistic and to better understand what they miss.

Safeguards

Cybersecurity and biology safeguards. Consistent with previous Claude Fable models, Fable 5.2 comes with safety classifiers that block high-risk cyber activities, including penetration testing, exploit generation, and binary-based vulnerability, as well as most tasks in research biology. When a query is blocked, users will instead receive a response from Opus 4.8 for cybersecurity and Opus 5 for biology. Since the release of Claude Fable 5.1, we have continued to reduce false positives for our safety classifiers. Based on early testing across claude.ai, Claude Code, and Cowork, we observed about 55% fewer blocks with Fable 5.2 compared with Fable 5.1—about 60% fewer in cybersecurity a [truncated for CSV - full text is in the JSON export]
