JPMorganChase is rolling out Claude across the firm, to more employees beyond engineers. In the Commercial and Investment Bank, work moves into production faster, and the firm redeploys that capacity against its business priorities.

Teams are modernizing other legacy systems, and engineers are building their own agents, including pull request review and self-healing agents, and sharing what works.

Infrastructure and operations teams use Claude Code (opens in new tab) for monitoring, alerting and root cause analysis. The firm's security team uses our frontier models to find and fix vulnerabilities faster, work we first described in Project Glasswing (opens in new tab).

Reaching product teams and advisors

The people closest to the business are building with Claude too. Product teams turn requirements directly into engineering backlogs, and other teams use Claude Code for risk and controls assessments and program planning.

Knowledge work is already underway. Much of the product development lifecycle happens outside the code: research, requirements, design and planning.

In their Asset & Wealth Management business, JPMorganChase is putting the people with the deepest business insight and the boldest ideas alongside their technology and product experts into small, empowered teams. This is helping them to more easily build and deliver customized client investment solutions at scale. Claude Code is now part of their engineering workflow, and teams are moving faster while putting every change through more rigorous testing before it reaches clients.

Last month, J.P. Morgan Asset Management announced a connector that brings 55ip's ActiveTax Technology® into Claude for Financial Advisors (opens in new tab), putting tax-aware portfolio transition analysis into advisors' daily work.

Built for a regulated firm

Claude Code runs in controlled environments, including Devspace, the firm’s containerized development platform, on its own infrastructure. The intent is to prevent agents from getting direct access to employee credentials or internal systems. Access widens in stages, and new Claude models go through the firm’s own approval process before anyone there can use them.

Code ships under the same discipline. Thousands of automated tests and approval gates check every change, and an automated gate returns a hard pass or halt that the pipeline enforces, so Claude can't sign off on its own work. People stay accountable for every production change.

Over the past year, JPMorganChase’s use of Claude has grown from software engineering to cyber defense to tools for financial advisors, and what JPMorganChase asks of us is shaping what we build for other regulated institutions. Claude working inside the controls of one of the world’s largest financial institutions is what we are building toward.

In this article

Mitigation and protection guidance

Microsoft Defender detections

Hunting queries

Indicators of compromise

In October 2026, the financially motivated threat actor Storm-3358 began targeting organizations in the financial sector using the agentic AI offensive framework ARTEX. The threat actor that Microsoft Threat Intelligence tracks as Storm-3358 is a Cambodia-based intrusion cluster that primarily targets financial organizations in Southeast Asia, in addition to a smaller number of large financial organizations globally.

Microsoft has observed Storm-3358 use ARTEX in combination with conventional automated tools to scan systems connected to the public internet, exploit security flaws including anonymous file upload and server-side request forgery (SSRF), and install open-source remote access trojans (RATs). Storm-3358 has used the WISP, vshell, and AdaptixC2 RATs for persistence and lateral movement. Microsoft has observed ARTEX agents using utilities like netcat and curl to download these RATs to compromised systems, as shown in Figure 1.

Figure 1. Example commands that ARTEX agents used to download RATs to compromised systems.

In recent ARTEX-related attacks, threat actors have used ARTEX agents to scan and exploit vulnerabilities in web applications, use web shells for persistence on compromised web servers, compromise credentials from public sources and compromised systems, and use compromised cloud identities for persistence and data exfiltration. ARTEX agents can also perform brute-force password attacks, password spraying, API enumeration and abuse, and database dumping. Agentic tools like ARTEX can leverage compromised credentials and systems at machine speed to move laterally, escalate privileges, and exfiltrate data.

This activity illustrates an ongoing trend of threat actors accelerating all stages of the attack chain with agentic AI penetration testing frameworks, including ARTEX. As these capabilities evolve, defenders must similarly use AI to investigate and respond across large environments.

While threat actors regularly use proxies and virtual private networks (VPNs) to change the source IP address of malicious traffic and bypass static detections, Microsoft is providing indicators of compromise (IOCs) to help defenders detect related activity.

Mitigation and protection guidance

Microsoft’s research into threats involving agentic frameworks informs security detections and investigative context across its products. The capabilities available to customers depend on the source of the activity and the products and protections deployed in their environment.

Several behavioral signals can help organizations determine that they are being targeted by threat actors using agentic AI. Agentic AI frameworks scanning a target send a wide variety of requests in a brief time and retry variations on the same technique or move on to next-stage actions at machine speed. Agentic AI frameworks use existing penetration testing tools. For example, ARTEX by default uses Nmap, curl, wget, Python HTTP clients, Norma SDK WebFetch, and headless Chromium through Playwright, among others. These tools may send network traffic with distinctive characteristics, such as default user agent strings. While blocking network traffic with these characteristics will not stop an attack by an AI agent, which will quickly change them, identifying them can alert defenders to the activity.

Defensive honeypots, decoys, tarpits, and fake wins can pull autonomous AI attacks away from legitimate targets. Honeypots and decoy surfaces such as Microsoft Sentinel Deception give the agent attractive but worthless targets to pursue. Tarpits consume the agent’s time and budget. Fake wins present convincing evidence that the agent’s objective is complete, which can cause it to stop on a false success. In Microsoft’s testing, these controls helped reduce the attack traffic reaching real assets and produced high-confidence, attribution-quality signal.

For additional information on the evolution of threat actors’ use of ARTEX please see Microsoft’s recent blogs: AI-driven, large-scale nation-state campaign using ARTEX enables supply chain compromise and Threat actors use agentic AI tooling to find and abuse exposed secrets.

Microsoft’s continuous research into threat actors leveraging agentic frameworks integrates directly into the following products:

Identity and sign-in activity — Microsoft Entra ID Protection

Microsoft analyzes sign-in activity and other signals to identify potential identity risk. Customers can investigate risk detections and risky sign-ins, and configure Conditional Access policies that use sign-in or user risk to require multifactor authentication or block access when specified conditions are met. Identity and sign-in activity from known threat actor infrastructure, including from agentic frameworks like ARTEX, generate Verified threat actor IP risk detections delivered at high risk. See:

Risk-based user sign-in protection in Microsoft Entra ID

Endpoint alerts help security teams identify and investigate suspicious activity on devices. Indicators of compromise can support detection and, when configured, blocking. Customers can review related alerts in the Microsoft Defender portal. See:

Review alerts in Microsoft Defender for Endpoint

Activity across security domains — Microsoft Defender portal

The portal brings together alerts and incidents from Microsoft security solutions and provides relevant threat intelligence to support investigation, threat hunting, and response. This helps customers assess suspicious activity in the context of their own environment. See:

Investigate alerts in Microsoft Defender XDR

Threat actor misuse of AI accelerates risk across enterprise environments by amplifying existing threats such as exploitation of vulnerabilities, phishing, malware threats, and insider activity. To help organizations stay ahead of AI-enabled threat activity, Microsoft has introduced the Security Dashboard for AI. The dashboard provides users with a unified view of AI security posture by aggregating security, identity, and data risk across Microsoft Defender, Microsoft Entra, and Microsoft Purview. See:

Microsoft Security Copilot is embedded in Microsoft Defender and provides security teams with AI-powered capabilities to summarize incidents, analyze files and scripts, summarize identities, use guided responses, and generate device summaries, hunting queries, and incident reports.

November 6, 2026

Partnerships are a core part of how GuidePoint serves customers. Our partners give us a direct view of what customers need, where the market is moving and which technologies can create meaningful value. As GuidePoint enters its next stage of growth, we want to make it easier for partners to work with us at the pace our customers expect.

"The best partnerships are built on access: to the right people, the right information and a shared view of where customers are headed. The Partner Portal gives our partners that access in one place, so together we can move faster and bring the right capabilities to the customers we serve."

— Mark Thornberry, Chief Business Officer, GuidePoint Security

The GuidePoint Partner Portal is part of that investment. It gives partners better ways to engage with teams across the company, understand our capabilities and build on opportunities to support shared customers.

We designed the portal around your feedback. Here’s what it means for your team.

Navigate at Scale

Our regional model puts local expertise and customer relationships at the center of how we do business. Each of our eight regions brings knowledge of its market and the customers we serve together.

Vendor partners have asked for an easier way to navigate that model as their business with GuidePoint grows. The portal helps you find the right resources, the first time, across the entire organization, giving your team the information it needs to connect beyond the relationships you already have.

See How Our Services and Your Technology Align

You may know GuidePoint through a particular customer engagement, technology partnership or regional relationship. The portal helps you see the broader range of our cybersecurity services and how we position technology within those areas.

That context can help your team better understand where your solutions fit, align with how GuidePoint supports customers and identify ways to bring more value to the customers we serve together. When we understand each other’s strengths, we can develop an opportunity, prove it works and scale it together.

Stay Connected

Knowing what’s happening across GuidePoint makes it easier to plan your involvement.

The portal brings many programs and activities into one actively updated calendar. Your team can look ahead at events in the markets you support and more easily identify opportunities to spend time with our teams.

Vendor all-hands recordings will live here too, so colleagues who couldn’t attend can catch up and stay informed.

Find Marketing and Event Resources

Looking for GuidePoint’s brand or marketing guidelines, logos or media kit? The portal brings these resources together in one place, along with lead follow-up best practices for GuidePoint events. You’ll also find thought leadership resources that showcase our work and the cybersecurity challenges we’re helping customers solve.

Built for You, Managed by Us

Our team manages the portal and keeps its resources current, so there’s nothing for you to upload, update or maintain. That’s intentional. We want the portal to save your team time and we’ll keep adding resources as our work together grows.

Get Started

The portal is now available for all vendor partners who hold an active reseller agreement with GuidePoint Security. Eligible vendor partners have received an email invitation with instructions for setting up an account.

If you’re interested in becoming a GuidePoint Security vendor partner, connect with our Vendor Relationship Management team to learn more.

Thank you to the partners whose feedback helped shape this resource. We look forward to building on it as our partnerships grow!

Title: Introducing AWS account access manager: IAM role flexibility with centralized workforce access
Context: Account access manager launch partners Account access manager launches with a broad ecosystem of AWS identity and access-governance partners who have integrated the service into...
Full Text:
AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) is introducing account access manager, a flexible new way to manage workforce access to your Amazon Web Services (AWS) accounts. This combines the IAM role flexibility your teams already rely on, delivered through the centralized federation of AWS IAM Identity Center, with user-level visibility built-in.

Account access manager streamlines the assignment of your existing IAM roles from individual AWS accounts to your workforce users and groups in an organization instance of IAM Identity Center, giving you a clear path to centralized access management at scale. You can adopt account access manager on its own or alongside IAM Identity Center permission sets; both draw on the same users and groups you already synchronize from your corporate identity provider. That means you assign your existing IAM roles to those users and groups directly, without duplicating identities or managing per-account federation points.

Why use account access manager?

Enterprises scaling on AWS have long faced a difficult choice in workforce access: the flexibility of IAM roles or the central control of IAM Identity Center. Until now, granting workforce access to AWS accounts generally meant choosing one of two approaches, each with trade-offs to consider. Federating into each account separately with IAM roles gives you the full flexibility of IAM roles—custom trust policies, tags, and paths—but requires you to configure an identity provider and manage role assignments independently in each account, making it harder to assign a group across multiple accounts or maintain a unified view of who has access where. Federating once through IAM Identity Center with permission sets gives you a single federation point with centrally provisioned, uniform access, but permission sets can feel restrictive for teams whose roles vary from account to account, or that have difficulty generalizing their existing roles into uniform sets.

Account access manager removes the trade-offs. It’s built for customers who want the single federation point and identity-propagation benefits of IAM Identity Center together with the flexibility of IAM roles. Because it uses the IAM roles you already own, you keep the tailoring capabilities you rely on today:

Attribute-based access control (ABAC) – Use IAM role tags, or session tags populated from your identity provider as SAML claims, for fine-grained, attribute-driven authorization.

Precise trust policies – Restrict role assumption with network conditions or identity provider (IdP)-asserted claims, such as group membership, department, or cost center, as trust-policy conditions.

Role paths for organization at scale – Use IAM role paths to group roles and simplify administration as your environment grows.

Because roles are managed in the account you provision access to, account access manager scales with your account usage rather than relying on Identity Center specific quotas. Assignments are made to users and groups, reducing administrative overhead, and providing accountability and auditability to the specific user and role being used.

How it works

Access flows through IAM Identity Center and carries the user’s identity through trusted identity propagation. Even when multiple users assume a shared IAM role, each role session contains user context that attributes every action to the individual user. Access is granted and audited against the actual user, so you can see who assumed which role in which account. The result is user-level visibility across your organization, not just at the point of sign-in. You also maintain access to the full set of IAM role capabilities, such as role paths, tagging, naming conventions, and other IAM primitives.

Figure 1: Account access manager connects IAM Identity Center federated workforce users and groups to AWS accounts specific IAM roles

To grant a user access to a specific role in an account using account access manager, an administrator creates an entitlement. The user can then access that account from the new account access manager application portal or from their IAM Identity Center access portal, or retrieve credentials from the command line with aws login.

You can manage account access manager through the AWS Management Console for IAM and programmatically through the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) (aws login and the account-access API namespace), AWS SDKs, AWS CloudFormation, and HashiCorp Terraform and Pulumi, so you can enable it and manage role assignments the same way you manage the rest of your AWS infrastructure. It exposes its own API namespace, account-access, separate from the IAM API, with its own permissions and AWS CloudTrail events.

How to enable account access manager

Here’s how to enable account access manager in your own environment, from prerequisites through your first role assignment.

Prerequisites

An organization instance of IAM Identity Center enabled.

Users or groups in IAM Identity Center that you want to entitle with IAM roles from individual AWS accounts. If users or groups don’t exist already then either:

Connect Identity Center to your external identity provider to automatically provision your corporate identities into Identity Center using SCIM.

Create users and groups in the Identity Center directory.

IAM roles in the individual AWS accounts that you want to assign to users and groups of IAM Identity Center. If the role you need doesn’t exist, create a role using custom trust policies first.

Appropriate permissions to enable account access manager and manage assignments (see the IAM policy examples later in this post).

Both the organization instance of IAM Identity Center and account access manager must be enabled in your organization’s management account.

For CLI access: Install or update to the latest version of the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) v2.36.0 or newer.

Step 1: Enable account access manager

Before enabling account access manager, run the following command from the AWS organization management account to grant account access manager access to your organization:

aws organizations enable-aws-service-access --service-principal account-access.amazonaws.com

Next, use one of the following methods to enable account access manager:

Console:

Sign in to your organization’s management account.

In the AWS Management Console for IAM navigation pane, under Multi-account access, choose account access manager.

The console Region should be set to the primary Region of your IAM Identity Center instance.

If there is no organization instance of IAM Identity Center, you’ll be prompted to enable one before continuing. Otherwise, choose Enable account access manager.

Figure 2: Account access manager enablement from the IAM console

AWS CLI:

Fetch the Amazon Resource Name (ARN) of your IAM Identity Center organization instance, confirm the Region code matches its primary Region, and run:

aws account-access create-application \ --region <Region> \ --identity-source '{ "identityCenter": { "instanceArn": "<IAM Identity Center Instance ARN>" } }'

As an output, the account access manager application ARN will be generated.

After you enable account access manager (through the console or AWS CLI), you will get the account access URL and the account access manager ARN along with other details on the capability.

Account access portal URL is the single sign-on entry point for your workforce. This is where your users will go to access AWS accounts. Its format is - https://[Tenant-ID].account-access.[Region].app.aws , found on the Settings tab of the account access manager console.

Account access manager ARN: the identifier for the application instance created when you enable account access manager. Note this ARN to use in your IAM role’s trust policies so that only your specific account access manager application can assume those roles, providing confused-deputy protection (see Step 3 for details) and pass it as --application-arn when creating entitlements using the AWS CLI so each assignment is tied to the correct application instance.

Figure 3: Account access manager settings after enablement

In the AWS CLI, run the command aws account-access list-applications to get the application ARN and tenant-ID of the enabled account access manager instance ARN.

Step 2: Update firewalls and gateways

If you filter access to specific AWS domains or URL endpoints with a next-generation firewall (NGFW) or Secure Web Gateway (SWG), allowlist the account access portal domains and endpoints in the following list. Account access manager has no IPv4-only endpoints; endpoints are dual-stack.

Account access portal URL – https://[Tenant-ID].account-access.[Region].app.aws

Portal APIs – [Tenant-ID].account-access.[Region].app.aws/api/* and /auth/*

Control plane – account-access.[Region].api.aws

Runtime – account-access-runtime.[Region].api.aws

Console – console.aws.amazon.com/account-access

Step 3: Prepare your IAM roles

Before assigning IAM roles to users and groups, update the role’s trust policy to allow account access manager service to assume it.

Add the following statement to the role’s trust policy (or paste the entire policy that follows if you’re creating a new role). Replace <your-account-id>, <region> (your IAM Identity Center primary Region), and <application-id> (from the Settings page of the console).

Figure 4: Account access manager ARN details

IAM role trust policy:

{ "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Sid": "AccountAccessManagerIAMRoleTrustPolicyStatement", "Effect": "Allow", "Principal": { "Service": "account-access.amazonaws.com" }, "Action": [ "sts:AssumeRole", "sts:SetContext", "sts:TagSession" ], "Condition": { "StringEquals": { "aws:SourceAccount": "<your-account-id>", "aws:SourceArn": "arn:aws:account-access:<region>:<your-account-id>:application/<application-id>" } } } ] }

Define the Condition block to enforce confused-deputy protection. It helps ensure that the role can be assumed only by the specific account access manager application instance (defined using the application ARN) created when you enabled the service, and only when the request originates from your AWS account where that instance resides.

Best practice:

Propagate identity attributes with ABAC – The sts:TagSession action listed in the preceding IAM role trust policy allows upstream attributes from your identity provider (group memberships, department, cost center) to flow through as principal tags on the session. Without it, role assumption still succeeds; only session-tag propagation is suppressed. Add it when downstream IAM policies use aws:PrincipalTag/<key> and the tag is populated from your IdP SAML claims; leave it out otherwise.

Automate the trust-policy update – We recommend updating your IAM role-creation workflows to add this trust-policy statement automatically wherever it’s needed, so new roles are assignable from day one. You can use this sample-aam-migration tool as a reference.

Step 4: Assign access to users and groups

Like IAM Identity Center role entitlements, an entitlement in account access manager requires three components: a user or group ID, an account ID, and an IAM role ARN (instead of a permission set ARN). You can create assignments from the Accounts, Users, or Groups tabs in the console, or using the API or AWS CLI. For assignments where the same role needs to be assigned to multiple users, you must create each assignment individually. You can automate it using the account access API, the AWS SDK, or AWS CLI.

Assign from the console:

Choose the Users tab and search by username or display name.

Select the user, then choose Assign new access.

Figure 5: Assign new access in account access manager

On the Assign account access page, enter the workforce user or group, account ID, and IAM role name, then choose Assign access.

Assign a user using AWS CLI:

aws account-access create-entitlement \ --region <Region> \ --application-arn "<Account_access_manager_ARN>" \ --entitlement '{ "principalRole": { "principal": { "identityCenter": { "userId": "<Identity_Center_User_ID>" } }, "roleArn": "arn:aws:iam::<ACCOUNT_ID>:role/<ROLE_NAME>" } }'

To assign a group, replace the userId block with "groupId": "<IDC_GROUP_ID>". To remove access, use aws account-access delete-entitlement with the entitlement ID.

Note:

The console can search users, groups, and accounts, but it can’t detect IAM roles because they can come from different AWS accounts in your organization; you must know the role name beforehand.

Only IAM roles whose trust policy grants account access manager as an allowed service principal are eligible for assignment.

IAM role sessions assigned by account access manager use the maximum session duration configured on the underlying IAM role in each AWS account, up to 12 hours.

Step 5: How workforce users can sign in

Workforce users can federate to AWS accounts using IAM roles assigned through account access manager in any of the following ways:

Directly through the account access portal URL – Navigate to the portal URL (for example, https://aa-xxxxxxxxx.account-access.us-east-2.app.aws, or a vanity URL) and sign in.

Through the AWS access portal – Go to the Applications tab, select the Account Access application, and you’ll be redirected to the account access portal, where your assigned accounts and their respective roles are listed.

Tip: We recommend that users bookmark both the account access portal and the AWS access portal for faster navigation. In addition, if you use a supported IdP, such as Okta, Microsoft Entra ID, or Ping Identity, you can add the account access portal as a bookmark app in the IdP’s dashboard, giving users authenticated, single-click access to the portal directly from the tools they already sign in to each day.

Access through a web browser

Use the following steps to use account access manager through a web browser.

Navigate to the account access portal URL and sign in with your credentials.

On the portal, find the AWS account you need. Search by account name or ID to filter the list of accounts you’re assigned to.

Expand the account to see the roles you can assume.

Select a role (for example, Developer). A new tab opens, signed into that account with the selected role.

Access through the AWS CLI

Account access manager works with the aws login command. To get started:

Install the latest AWS CLI (v2.36.0 or newer).

Sign in through your default browser – Sign in to your account access portal and into the target AWS account using one of your assigned roles.

On the AWS CLI, run:

aws login

Set a default Region if prompted – If you haven’t set one, the AWS CLI will prompt you for a Region (for example, us-east-2).

Select your session – The AWS CLI opens a browser page; select the tile for the session you initiated.

Confirm and return to the CLI – The page confirms that your credentials were shared successfully. Close the tab and keep working in the AWS CLI for the duration of your session.

The temporary credentials are automatically rotated by the AWS CLI, AWS Tools for PowerShell, and AWS SDKs, and remain valid for the default session duration of an IAM role. After the session expires, you’re prompted to sign in again on the browser.

Note: IAM Identity Center–specific commands, such as aws sso configure, don’t work with account access manager assignments; use aws login instead. If you want to continue to use aws sso login, refer to AWS CLI Integration for IAM Account access manager.

Create shortcut links to specific console destinations

The portal also lets you create a shortcut link that opens a specific console destination for a given account and role. Shortcut links work only with accounts and roles already assigned to the user—they can’t grant new access—and URL parameters must be URL-encoded. Because shortcut links are Regional and expose the account ID and role name in plain text, review your organization’s sharing policies before experimenting with them.

Customer managed key considerations

If your IAM Identity Center instance is encrypted with an AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) customer managed key, which is required when you replicate IAM Identity Center to additional Regions, check the key policy before you enable account access manager. We recommend implementing the current baseline KMS key policy to ensure account access manager can read user, group, and instance data from IAM Identity Center.

Best practices summary

Enable in the right place – Enable account access manager in your organization’s management account and in the same Region as your IAM Identity Center instance and confirm your organization instance is in place before you begin.

Automate trust-policy updates – Build the account access manager trust-policy statement into your role-creation pipelines so every new role is assignable from day one, with no manual intervention.

Add sts:TagSession only when you need it – Include it only where downstream policies consume principal tags; otherwise leave it off to keep sessions lean and least-privilege.

Assign roles to groups, not individual users – Granting access at the group level reduces administrative overhead and strengthens the auditability of user-level access.

Scope administrator permissions tightly – Separate managing the feature from managing assignments, and enable delegating administration to keep day-to-day operations out of the management account.

Allowlist the portal domains before rollout – Add the account access portal domains and endpoints to your next-generation firewall or Secure Web Gateway ahead of launch to avoid access disruptions.

Prepare your workforce users – Have users bookmark both the account access portal and the AWS access portal and communicate the aws login flow clearly to your developers.

Account access manager launch partners

Account access manager launches with a broad ecosystem of AWS identity and access-governance partners who have integrated the service into their existing solutions, making it available to our joint customers from day one. Leading identity providers Okta, PingIdentity and Cisco Duo extend account access manager so customers can manage human workforce access to AWS accounts directly from the identity platforms they already use. Alongside them, access-governance and privileged-access partners Apono, BeyondTrust, Britive, Sonrai Security, C1.ai and Lumos added capabilities to govern, provision, and audit that access through the tooling our customers already rely on.

Account access manager also integrates with leading infrastructure-as-code (IaC) partners, so teams can define and manage access assignments declaratively alongside the rest of their AWS infrastructure. Pulumi enables customers to codify account access manager role assignments as part of their existing provisioning workflows, bringing repeatable, version-controlled automation to workforce access at scale.

Conclusion

Account access manager combines the flexibility of the IAM roles your teams already own with the single, centralized federation point of IAM Identity Center, adding user-level visibility into what users or roles have done across your organization. You assign existing IAM roles to users and groups centrally, scale with your account usage rather than a fixed quota, and give developers a fast, secure command-line experience with aws login. It’s available at no additional cost, enabled by default in Commercial Regions (excluding opt-in Commercial Regions, GovCloud (US), China, and other non-commercial Regions).

To see account access manager in action, watch the enablement video, which walks through enabling the service, preparing your IAM roles, and assigning access to your workforce end to end. You can also extend account access manager through our launch partners; leading identity, access-governance, and IaC providers who have integrated the service into their platforms, so you can govern, provision, and automate workforce access to AWS using the tooling you already rely on. Review the preceding partner integrations to find the ones that fit your environment.

To learn more and get started, visit the AWS Identity and Access Management User Guide. We encourage you to enable account access manager in a test organization, assign your first entitlement, and explore how centralized, user-attributed access can simplify your AWS environment.

Title: Introducing Personal Finance in Claude
Context: Access is read-only, and Personal Finance can’t move, manage, or invest your money
Full Text:
Getting answers about your money no longer means opening every banking app and doing the math yourself. With Personal Finance in Claude, you can securely connect your bank and card accounts and ask in your own words. Access is read-only, and Personal Finance can’t move, manage, or invest your money.

Claude gives you answers in everyday language, from your balances and transactions, and explains any term that's new to you. Like the rest of Claude, Personal Finance has no ads or sponsored recommendations, and it doesn’t offer credit cards, loans, or savings accounts of its own, so your money questions get a straight answer.

Personal Finance starts rolling out in beta this week, on the Pro, Max, and Ultra plans in the US.

What it looks like

Say it's late in the month and payday is still 10 days away. When you ask Claude, "Where did my money go this month?" it adds up your spending across the accounts you connected and sorts it by category. In this example, that comes to $4,309.37, with more than half going to rent and utilities and $1,024.51 to food and drink.

From there, you can dig deeper: "Is that more than usual?" "Anything else I'm missing?" "So what's left before payday?" Claude checks the previous months and points to a membership renewal. Then Claude tells you about four payments that will come out of your checking account before payday, and what you’ll have left: $1,393.22.

If you ask whether anything looks off, Claude reads across every account you've connected and can point to what's easy to miss, like charges that hit twice, unexpected fees, or a bill that’s crept up all year. You can also ask bigger questions, like "Am I spending more than I make?" or "What's an APR, and what has mine cost me this year?" Claude explains the term, then adds up the interest you've been charged.

Ask for a weekly spending chart, a calendar of what's due, or a dashboard of the numbers you choose, and Claude builds one you can keep adjusting.

Security and privacy

Claude's access is read-only. Personal Finance helps you understand your money, and it isn't designed to give investment advice. Claude can make mistakes in its answers, so ask which transactions are behind a number, and check important figures with your bank.

Your accounts are only connected once you sign in to your bank yourself through Plaid, a service that connects apps to banks. That's where you agree to its terms and approve Claude's read-only access, so Claude doesn't ask for or see your bank password.

For the accounts you choose to connect (and only those), Claude sees the bank's name, each account's name, type, and last four digits, balances and credit limits, and up to two years of transactions. When you chat with Claude in the Personal Finance hub, those conversations aren't used to train our models. For anything you share with Claude outside the hub, your privacy settings apply. You can unlink an account anytime, and then Claude can no longer see its data. More details can be found in our Privacy Center.

Getting started

When you see Personal Finance in Claude's sidebar, open it, connect one account, and ask a single question, like "Can I afford a trip this spring?" or "How much could I save each month?" You'll find the setup steps, and how your data is used and kept, in the Help Center. (opens in new tab)

What’s next

Personal Finance is a first step. For life’s bigger money decisions, we think people are best served by Claude working alongside the licensed professionals and regulated firms they trust. We’re exploring how to make that possible in Claude, and we’d like to hear from banks, wealth managers, and financial services companies who want to help shape it.

Title: CrowdStrike Extends the Agentic SOC to Detect and Stop Agent Insider Threats
Context: This foundation extends to the place many of these attacks begin: the AI tooling agents depend on
Full Text:
When individual signals are brought together, a clear picture forms. With Dynamic Risk Scoring (Q4), agent risk feeds into the same 0 to 100 risk score that Falcon Next-Gen SIEM already builds for the agent's owner and host. When an agent, its user, and its device all climb the risk list together, the coordination behind otherwise routine activity is harder to miss.

This foundation extends to the place many of these attacks begin: the AI tooling agents depend on. AI Ecosystem Detections (Q4) add detection logic for attacks on AI services, including LLM API abuse, stolen API keys, and the compromise of coding assistants, MCP servers, and agent frameworks. When the threat starts in a trusted tool rather than the agent itself, the Falcon platform is watching there too.

Because the context around an agent doesn't always live inside the Falcon platform, Federated Search Expansion lets teams search related data where it already lives, without re-ingestion. New connectors for GovCloud, Dynatrace, Databricks, and Snowflake are now generally available, with Splunk, Elastic, and Cribl Lake connectors following in Q4.

Act on Tough Questions

Once a risky agent surfaces, every analyst faces the same question: Did an agent’s owner do this, or did their agent do it without them knowing?

This is the work Multi-Agent Triage and Investigation (GA, announced at Fal.Con US 2026) was built for. SOC agents investigate detections end to end, with specialist agents working the case together on shared context across endpoint, identity, and the agent's activity.

Investigation coverage already spans the full range of Falcon platform and third-party sources. In Q4, triage coverage extends to CrowdStrike Falcon® Guardian, CrowdStrike Falcon® Cloud Security, CrowdStrike Falcon® Shield, CrowdStrike Falcon® Data Security, and custom detections, including abnormal agent behavior flagged by Falcon Next-Gen SIEM. When an agent is flagged, it routes straight into an agentic investigation where the agent, its owner, and its host are already connected.

This shared context is what answers the tough question. Investigating agents can trace a session back to what the person asked for and separate it from what the agent did on its own. When the person's request was routine and everything that followed traces to instructions they never wrote, the verdict becomes clear: The insider was the agent, not the employee.

But a verdict doesn't stop a compromised agent that's still running. The Unified Agentic SOAR Experience (GA, announced at Fal.Con US 2026) is where response happens. Teams build, run, and govern all automation in the SOC, from AI agents to workflows to custom apps, in plain language. They set the mission and define triggers, data, rules, and actions to decide what runs autonomously and what requires approval. A single response decision can coordinate everything that needs to follow in parallel: stopping the agent, cutting off its access, keeping it from coming back, and documenting what happened. It's open by design and connects to any agent, model, or tool through API or MCP, so teams can govern automation across the security stack with visibility into what it's costing and what needs attention.

See it in action:

Autonomy That Earns Its Trust

As SOCs hand more of the work to agents, the controls that keep agents accountable matter as much as the speed they deliver.

CrowdStrike builds governance into every layer of the agentic SOC. It starts by watching the SOC's agents. Policy-Drift Agent Guardrails, powered by Falcon Guardian (Beta, Q4), screen every CrowdStrike Charlotte AI™ and AgentWorks interaction for policy drift, unauthorized tool calls, and out-of-bounds data access to catch the moment an agent steps outside its intended scope.

Title: CrowdStrike Introduces Agentic Adversary Emulation to Counter AI-Enabled Adversaries
Context: Attack Path Discovery to Validated Defense Reveal Potential Attack Paths Instead of simply identifying vulnerabilities, Agentic Adversary Emulation shows how attackers could...
Full Text:
Frontier AI is enabling threat actors to rapidly learn an environment, identify weaknesses, and chain them into viable paths to critical systems. These capabilities allow adversaries to move faster while exploiting vulnerabilities, misconfigurations, and other gaps to achieve their goals.

Traditional exposure management helps organizations identify and prioritize weaknesses largely as individual risks, and periodic red team engagements only provide deeper validation at a point in time. Neither approach alone can continuously validate defenses at the speed and scale of AI-enabled adversaries. Organizations must understand not only where they are exposed, but what adversaries could achieve and whether corrective actions can strengthen their defenses.

To fight AI-enabled adversaries with AI, CrowdStrike is introducing Agentic Adversary Emulation, a new AI-powered red teaming capability powered by CrowdStrike® SafeMind. It’s now in early access.

Agentic Adversary Emulation combines specialized AI models and offensive harnesses with real-world adversary intelligence and deep knowledge of customer environments. Operating within controlled, customer-approved boundaries in production environments, it uncovers exploitable attack paths, generates prioritized remediation recommendations and compensating controls, and validates whether corrective actions have strengthened defenses.

Attack Path Discovery to Validated Defense

Reveal Potential Attack Paths

Instead of simply identifying vulnerabilities, Agentic Adversary Emulation shows how attackers could exploit and chain weaknesses across systems and identities to compromise critical assets, and where defenses can stop them. This helps security teams understand what attackers could accomplish in their environment.

Turn Findings into Defensive Action

Agentic Adversary Emulation translates these exploitable attack paths into prioritized remediation actions and compensating controls that security teams can review and deploy through the CrowdStrike Falcon® platform. These may include applying patches, changing configurations, updating security policies, and creating new detections. By connecting demonstrated attack paths to corrective actions, this helps organizations focus on the weaknesses attackers can exploit and take targeted action to disrupt their progress.

Verify that Fixes Work

After corrective actions are implemented, Agentic Adversary Emulation repeats the attack simulation to verify whether those changes successfully disrupt previously identified attack paths. This helps organizations determine whether their fixes work and whether security controls can prevent adversaries from advancing toward critical assets. By connecting attack path discovery, remediation, and validation, Agentic Adversary Emulation creates a closed loop across offense and defense: attack, defend, and validate.

The CrowdStrike Advantage in AI-Powered Red Teaming

Agentic Adversary Emulation combines three core CrowdStrike capabilities to bring real-world adversary behavior into AI-powered red team testing:

Industry-leading adversary intelligence: CrowdStrike pioneered adversary-driven threat intelligence and tracks more than 290 adversaries globally. Recognized as a Leader by both Gartner and Forrester in threat intelligence, CrowdStrike draws on frontline threat hunting, incident response, CrowdStrike Falcon® platform telemetry, and intelligence on emerging threats to bring the latest adversary tradecraft directly into red team testing.

Deep knowledge of customer environments: The Falcon platform provides rich context across assets, identities, vulnerabilities, configurations, and security controls. This enables CrowdStrike to go beyond generic attack scenarios to emulate how adversaries could exploit interconnected weaknesses in a customer's environment to gain access to critical systems.

Powered by CrowdStrike SafeMind: SafeMind provides the purpose-built AI models and offensive harnesses that drive Agentic Adversary Emulation. Combining CrowdStrike’s latest adversary intelligence with deep visibility into customer environments, these systems emulate real-world adversary behavior at machine speed, continuously exploring attack paths and adapting as new weaknesses are discovered. Operating within customer-approved boundaries, they identify exploitable weaknesses, reveal how attackers could chain them together, and demonstrate what adversaries could achieve against critical assets.

During early access, CrowdStrike will work closely with selected customers to conduct controlled red teaming within defined safeguards and customer-approved boundaries, while refining the operational guardrails for safe execution in production environments.

Bringing Threat Intelligence to Smartphones

As AI accelerates adversary operations, security teams need trusted intelligence to make faster decisions, wherever they are. CrowdStrike is bringing its industry-leading threat intelligence and agentic AI capabilities to a new mobile app for iOS and Android. Available to CrowdStrike Falcon® Adversary Intelligence Premium customers, the app extends the Falcon experience beyond the desktop, providing direct access to the latest intelligence reports and the Threat Intelligence Agent.

Through the new app, customers can:

Stay ahead of emerging threats: Access expert-validated intelligence on adversaries, including their latest activities, evolving tactics, and emerging campaigns, to understand threats as they develop.

Act faster: Ask the Threat Intelligence Agent questions in natural language to quickly understand adversaries, campaigns, vulnerabilities, and emerging threats, identify what matters most, and determine what actions to take.

Make informed decisions anywhere: Access trusted intelligence and AI-driven analysis wherever decisions need to be made, without being tied to a desktop or the Falcon console.

Advancing Adversary-Driven Security for the AI Era

With Agentic Adversary Emulation and the new threat intelligence mobile app, CrowdStrike is expanding how organizations put adversary intelligence to work, from proactively simulating attacks and strengthening defenses to making informed security decisions wherever they are. Together, these innovations help defenders stay ahead of evolving threats through faster, more proactive, intelligence-driven security.

Title: Introducing Sysdig AI Defense: See, stop, and prove what agents do
Context: Same sensor codebase, same Falco rules for detections, same threat research
Full Text:
AI has moved from assisting to acting. Agents now read files, run commands and reach your cloud with a real person’s access. Most of the time, the only record of what they did is the one the agent wrote itself. “A First Look: Under the Hood of AI Agents” shows where one software company's agents logged one tool call for every seven processes the kernel actually watched them run. And it isn’t only engineers. Someone in finance can wire up a coding agent on a Tuesday afternoon. Every agent, model and seat they add becomes a line item most companies can’t trace to a team or a task.

Find every agent, decide what it can do, keep the record

Sysdig AI Defense is runtime security and governance for every AI agent your teams run, from the laptop where an agent starts its work to the cloud where its actions land.

It starts by showing you what’s there. It finds the agents, MCP servers, skills and plugins your people use, including the ones nobody approved, and ties each one to the account and the person behind it.

Then you decide what agents are allowed to do. Most of the time, nothing changes. Everything your policies don’t name runs as normal, so developers keep working. For the actions you care about, you pick the response. Confirm pauses the call and asks the developer to approve it first. Block refuses it outright. A kill process ends the work the moment the process starts.

Whatever happens, there’s a record. Every action Sysdig AI Defense sees lands in your Sysdig tenant, off the device, where the agent can’t change it. Security can prove what happened, and leaders can see which teams use which models for which work.

Under the hood, it’s the same runtime engine Sysdig built to protect cloud workloads. Same sensor codebase, same Falco rules for detections, same threat research. What’s new is where it looks. It now follows AI agents wherever they work.

By default, Sysdig AI Defense doesn't collect the prompts your people type or the agent's replies. File edits and tool results are removed before they leave the machine. Your data stays in your Sysdig tenant, in the region you choose.

See every agent and MCP server your teams run, then decide what they can use

The questions security leaders ask us most are simple: what agents are running, which ones has nobody approved, and who owns them? Most can't answer these questions yet. In a 2026 IBM study, 77% of organizations surveyed said AI adoption is already outpacing their governance, and two-thirds of the CIOs and CTOs said they are held accountable for AI systems they do not fully control. Sysdig AI Defense answers from what is actually running, across tools like Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and GitHub Copilot, and it follows agents across the whole AI fabric: employee workstations, production Linux and Kubernetes, and the managed agent platforms you don’t own.

Most security teams are likely running more agents than they know about. One software company with about 300 machines found that out in its first month on Sysdig AI Defense. Nothing was blocked, because every policy ran in Alert for the whole month. The full findings are in our “A First Look: Under the Hood of AI Agents”. Half the agents Sysdig AI Defense found on those machines were instances the security team didn’t know about. Employees had signed up with personal email addresses on company devices, outside single sign-on, and every device had at least one agent harness installed and in active use.

Shadow AI isn’t only unapproved agents, either. Early adopters reported finding Ollama, llama.cpp and LM Studio running on people’s machines, a Qwen coding model served locally, and models downloaded straight to laptops. None of that crosses your AI gateway, so the gateway never sees it. The kernel does. It sees each one install, start and pull a model, and ties it to the person behind it.

Once you can see it, you can decide what’s allowed. New AI tools show up in the inventory as they appear on devices. If you don’t want agents using an MCP server, or one of its tools, deny it and set the policy to Block. The agent’s call is refused before it runs, and the agent sees your reason. If there’s a service agents should never send data to, name it in a policy, and kill process ends the upload as the process starts.

‍

Let agents work, and stop only the action that goes too far

An allowlist makes it easy to stop what you already know you don't want. The action itself is harder to judge, because it happens in the middle of a job, often in a fraction of a second. Even the labs that build these models have watched their own agents cross a line. Both OpenAI and Anthropic have disclosed cases where agents working through test tasks reached real systems that belonged to someone else. So the check has to happen at the moment the agent acts. Block and Confirm policies step in on the agent’s tool call before it runs. Kill process catches any process the moment it starts, no matter which agent launched it. You choose which response each policy gets.

Take a file of customer records. Opening one is ordinary work for an agent, and most of the time it is fine. What matters is where the data goes next, and what the agent gave itself permission to do along the way. A read that stays on the machine passes without a second look. The same read, followed by an upload to a public file-sharing host by an agent that just widened its own permissions, is an incident.

When an agent is told no, it tries another route, like a shell command or a script it writes itself. A hook sees the command but is blind to the script. AI Defense sees both. It sees the command with its destination parsed out, and the script as it starts.

You don’t have to write policy from scratch. Start from Sysdig’s managed policies for the risks agents bring, such as MCP servers and tools, secrets and data, and destructive commands. Each one is written as Falco rules you can read. You also don’t have to turn on blocking on day one. Every Sysdig policy starts in Alert, which means it raises what it sees and stops nothing. Watch what it catches on your own fleet. Then choose Block, Confirm or Kill process for the actions that matter. For actions you want a human on, Confirm sends the call to the agent’s own permission prompt, so the developer approves or refuses it right where they’re already working. Security decides which actions need that second look. Everything else runs as normal.

Not every risk fits a rule written in advance. Agents pick up new skills all the time. That’s why Sysdig’s threat research rules also look for agent behavior that resembles an attack, like credential dumping, persistence, tunnels and remote access.

Here’s what that looks like in our demo environment. A revenue operations agent, running with approvals turned off, tries to send a customer export to a public file host. A Kill process policy ends the upload as it starts, and the agent tells the person why.

When security wants to see how it got there, session replay steps through the session’s tool calls in order. The detections and kills show up in the Events rows beside it, each naming the rule and policy that fired.

See which model tier each team uses, for which task

Because every agent is tied to a person, so is every model it uses. Each session carries the model it ran on and the person and team behind it, whether or not the traffic goes through an AI gateway.

That matters for AI spend. In the same findings, four in ten employees ran Opus-class models only. Sysdig AI Defense rates each person’s model tier against how demanding their work was, by team. It flags light work running on the most expensive models, so leaders can change the habit before the invoice shows up. It also flags heavy work on the cheapest models, where someone may be stuck with a model too light for the job. Managers can move them to a better fit and help them get more done.

Answer an audit without pulling developers off their work

When an auditor asks what an agent did and who was behind it, most teams have one place to look, which is the agent’s own log. That log can miss a lot.

The kernel is the part of the operating system every action passes through, which makes it a good place to check. “A First Look: Under the Hood of AI Agents” found that the agent’s own log had no entry for 82% of the credential-file reads the kernel recorded, and no entry for 95% of the reads the agent binary made itself. Across that month, the kernel recorded 2.6 million processes against 374,000 tool calls in the agents’ own logs. The agent’s log is useful context, but it leaves out too much to carry an audit on its own.

Sysdig AI Defense keeps its own record from the kernel, off the device, where the agent can't change it. Remove Sysdig AI Defense’s own hook and it puts it back within the hour, and the kernel keeps recording in between. Each event carries the agent, the account, the model and the session. Each detection names the rule and policy behind it. With Sysdig AI Defense, the evidence is already on file when an audit asks about AI, and nobody has to pull a developer off their work to rebuild it. Teams can also forward these records to their SIEM, where they sit with the rest of their security evidence.

Accountability for agents starts at runtime

Boards are asking what agents are doing, and regulators are starting to ask too. Hatem Naguib, Sysdig's CEO, has boiled it down to three questions every executive should be able to answer:

How do we know our AI isn't going rogue?

What AI are we using, and who is accountable for it?

What can we prove?

None of these can be answered from the agent's own log alone.

Sysdig AI Defense brings to agents the same prevention, detection, and response Sysdig delivers across the cloud, rooted in Falco, the open source runtime security project Sysdig created in 2016 and that the CNCF graduated in 2024. Falco has passed 200 million downloads and is used by more than 60% of the Fortune 500.

Agents will keep getting faster, and their actions will keep reaching deeper into the cloud. The companies that scale them with confidence will be the ones that put the controls in first: every agent known, owned, and tied to an identity; the risky actions stopped as they happen; and a record that holds up afterwards.

See it on your own fleet. Start a free trial and find out what your agents are really doing. Available for macOS and Windows. Sysdig AI Defense runs beside your EDR and can be deployed through your MDM. For the full picture, we recommend rolling it out to at least ten machines.

Most managed service providers (MSPs) have one place where everything about a client lives: their devices, passwords, network details, and the steps for onboarding a new user. For many MSPs, that place is Hudu.

Now your Huntress data can live there too. Hudu has built a Huntress integration that brings your Huntress organizations, agents, memberships, and identities into Hudu and matches them to the client records you already have. It's available now in beta.

Huntress data displayed in Hudu via the Huntress <> Hudu integration

This post covers what Hudu is, what the integration does, how to set it up, and how Hudu built it on the Huntress API.

What Is Hudu?

Hudu is an IT documentation platform for MSPs and internal IT teams. It keeps documentation, passwords, assets, and network details in one structured, searchable place, and more than 6,000 teams use it.

Hudu puts it this way: your PSA manages your work, your RMM manages your devices, and Hudu manages your knowledge. That means the context, credentials, and procedures behind everything those tools touch.

Hudu Dashboard when a user first logs in.

Every client in Hudu is documented with the same structure. That way, any technician can pick up any client without digging through old notes or relying on someone's memory. Hudu also connects with the PSAs, RMMs, and other tools MSPs already use, so that documentation stays accurate. Now Huntress is one of those tools.

How the Integration Works

Once it's set up, Huntress becomes part of each client's documentation in Hudu. A technician can open a client and see the Huntress side of that environment next to everything else:

Which devices have the Huntress agent

Who has access to the client's Huntress organization

Which identities Huntress is protecting

That cuts down on tab-switching during the workday. Say a technician is onboarding a new employee or troubleshooting a laptop. They can confirm Huntress coverage from the same page where they're already working, without logging in to a separate portal to look it up.

Huntress organizations with existing Hudu companies during integration setup.

Create a User API Key in Huntress.

Add your Huntress API credentials to the Huntress integration in Hudu.

Match your Huntress organizations to your Hudu companies.

Map Huntress data to the right asset types and fields in Hudu.

To create your API key, follow our Generating API Keys guide.

Huntress API Documentation portal where developers can find the info they need to build custom integrations.

For this integration, Hudu pulls data from the Huntress API's organization, agent, membership, and identity data. Combined with what Hudu already knows about each client, that gives technicians a fuller picture in one place.

The Huntress API gave us everything we needed to bring that security context right onto the client page, so technicians can see what's protected without leaving their documentation."

Jordan Hart

Director of Product, Hudu

One Kill Switch with Comprehensive Enforcement Points

Coming soon, CrowdStrike will extend AI Kill Switch beyond gateway enforcement to deliver coordinated agent containment across the Falcon platform.

AI agents operate across endpoints, cloud environments, SaaS applications, browsers, and enterprise identities, often spanning multiple environments in a single chain of activity. CrowdStrike's vision is one AI Kill Switch coordinating response across multiple enforcement points. This will bring together the security capabilities of the Falcon platform and its broader ecosystem to contain rogue agents wherever they operate, including:

Endpoint agents: Terminate rogue agents and associated processes directly on affected endpoints and prevent them from restarting.

Browser sessions: Leverage CrowdStrike Falcon® Seraphic® Enterprise Browser to terminate sessions and disrupt unauthorized activity through web applications.

With AI Kill Switch, CrowdStrike introduces a decisive new way to rapidly disrupt dangerous AI activity when risk emerges. This is the first step toward broader enforcement to coordinate containment across the endpoints, identities, cloud environments, SaaS applications, and browsers where agents operate.

The objective is simple: Give organizations the confidence to embrace AI, control its expanding attack surface, and stop threats before they become breaches.

Composer 2.11 Adds Dependency Cooldowns
Context: The release arrives nearly a year after developers first requested the feature, bringing Composer into line with package managers that have already adopted minimum release age...
Full Text:
Composer 2.11 has introduced dependency cooldowns, giving PHP developers a native way to delay newly published package versions before they become eligible for installation. The release arrives nearly a year after developers first requested the feature, bringing Composer into line with package managers that have already adopted minimum release age policies to reduce exposure to supply chain attacks.

The new config.policy.cooldown setting allows developers to specify a waiting period in hours, days, or weeks. It is disabled by default and applies during dependency resolution, including composer update and composer require. Existing lockfile installations remain unaffected.

The feature also supports organization-wide configuration through Private Packagist, which can enforce cooldowns regardless of the Composer version developers and CI systems are running.

Preventing Cooldown Bypasses #

The original GitHub issue opened in November 2025 and gained urgency following a series of high-profile supply chain compromises. An initial implementation was submitted in December, but the feature missed Composer 2.10 as the maintainers worked through how to enforce cooldowns reliably.

In May, after additional attacks affected Packagist, developers pressed the maintainers for an update. Composer co-founder Nils Adermann explained that the feature was being held up by changes needed to make release metadata trustworthy.

The existing time field in Composer package metadata could be derived from a Git commit date or supplied through composer.json. Both are under the publisher's control, allowing an attacker to backdate a malicious release and bypass a cooldown.

Packagist introduced a new published-time field in June, recording when a version first became available through the registry. Composer 2.11 now uses that timestamp rather than trusting dates supplied by package publishers. Repositories without the required metadata cause dependency resolution to fail unless an explicit fallback is configured.

The cooldown feature is part of a broader security effort by Composer and Packagist. In a May security update, maintainers specifically cited the April compromise of intercom/intercom-php, and the May attack on Laravel Lang among recent incidents affecting the PHP ecosystem. The update outlined several security initiatives, including malware detection, version immutability, and the planned cooldown policy.

Cooldowns Are Now Standard Across Package Ecosystems #

For years, dependency management favored staying on the latest compatible releases. That assumption is changing. With compromised packages appearing on a regular basis, living on the bleeding edge has become considerably less appealing. Cooldowns are increasingly treated as standard supply chain security practice, and some package managers have already made them the default.

Composer is joining a movement already well underway across JavaScript, Ruby, Python, and Rust tooling.

pnpm introduced minimum release ages in September 2025 and made a 24-hour delay the default in version 11. Yarn has also enabled a release-age gate by default, while npm and Bun offer configurable delays. GitHub introduced a three-day default cooldown for Dependabot version updates in July.

In Ruby, Bundler added cooldown support in June, and gem.coop began testing registry-level delays earlier this year. Cargo is next, with minimum publish age support scheduled to become stable in Rust 1.100 on November 12.

Unlike pnpm and Yarn, Composer is leaving the feature opt-in, a decision its maintainers debated during development over concerns about disrupting existing workflows.

Composer also deliberately avoids automatically exempting security fixes. The maintainers rejected that approach because an attacker with publishing access could potentially create an advisory or exploit an existing one to get a malicious release through the cooldown. Developers can use --no-cooldown to install an urgent fix immediately without disabling other security policies. Composer also supports permanent exemptions for specific packages through the cooldown policy's ignore setting.

Security fixes still demand quick updates, especially as AI-assisted vulnerability disclosures accelerate, but for routine dependency updates, cooldowns are becoming best practice. Composer's implementation arrives later than many of its peers, but its adoption adds another major ecosystem to the shift toward giving new dependencies time to be examined before installation.

Conclusion

This campaign illustrates how BITTER combines native Windows tools with custom malware to establish and maintain access to targeted systems. The other two chains deliver PapRAT through LNK files and MSI installers, enabling system reconnaissance, file manipulation, secondary payload delivery, screenshot capture, and remote command execution.

Cloudflare services for private origins is now generally available
Context: Today, Cloudflare services for private origins is generally available. Point a proxied DNS record at a private IP, and Cloudflare reaches the origin over your existing Cloudflare One connection<
Full Text:
Today, Cloudflare services for private origins is generally available. Point a proxied DNS record at a private IP, and Cloudflare reaches the origin over your existing Cloudflare One connection. Your origin stays private, while web application firewall (WAF), caching, bot management, and Workers work just as they do for public origins.

In June, we launched this capability in closed beta to address a problem we kept hearing from customers: Their internal APIs, AI agent backends, MCP servers, and operational tools weren’t built to face the Internet, but those services still need to accept requests from partners, customers, or agents over the Internet. Before the beta, putting Cloudflare in front of these services meant exposing a public IP, opening a firewall port, or running cloudflared alongside the origin.

Those requirements often left private applications without the same protections and controls they used for public applications, including WAF, bot management, rate limiting, caching, traffic acceleration, rewrites, and Workers.

What is generally available today

During the closed beta, eligible customers requested access through their account team. Today, we’re opening access beyond that beta group.

Point a proxied A or AAAA record at a private IP, and Cloudflare’s application services work as they do for public origins:

WAF and managed rules

Bot management

Rate limiting

Caching

Transform and rewrite rules

Workers

Some limitations remain. Argo Smart Routing and Dedicated CDN Egress IPs aren’t supported, and origin health checks require Load Balancing. See the developer documentation for the full list of current limitations.

Your origin keeps its private IP, with no inbound firewall exception required. With Cloudflare WAN, no connector software on the origin is required. With Cloudflare Mesh, a connector runs within your private network and can serve multiple origins.

How it works

Create a proxied A or AAAA record pointing to your origin. For supported private IP ranges, use private network routing is enabled automatically. If your origin uses a public IP that’s reachable only through your private network, you can enable the setting manually.

The rest of the request flow stays the same: TLS termination, WAF, rules, and caching continue to run on Cloudflare’s network.

The setting turns on automatically for RFC 1918 private IPv4 addresses, RFC 6598 CGNAT addresses (100.64.0.0/10), and RFC 4193 unique local IPv6 addresses (fc00::/7). It can’t be turned off for these ranges; attempts to disable it through the API return an error.

What the API looks like

For customers automating deployments through the API, private routing is simply an additional attribute on a standard DNS record.

POST /zones/{zone_id}/dns_records { "type": "A", "name": "app.example.com", "content": "10.0.0.50", "ttl": 300, "proxied": true, "private_routing": true }

Behind the scenes, Cloudflare's proxy platform determines where to send traffic for app.example.com by querying Cloudflare's Origin API. The response includes metadata indicating that the destination should be reached through a private network path:

{ "zone_name": "example.com", "ipv4_addresses": ["10.0.0.50"], "private_routing": true }

The private_routing flag is the key signal. When our proxy sees it, instead of attempting to connect directly to the private IP address over the public Internet, it hands the request to our private networking layer, which then routes the connection across the customer's existing private network connectivity, whether that's IPsec, GRE, Cloudflare Tunnel, CNI, or Cloudflare Mesh.

The beta post covers the routing layer in more detail.

Get started

Before you begin, you’ll need:

The Private Origins entitlement on your account. Ask your account team to turn it on.

Cloudflare One connectivity using IPsec, GRE, CNI, Cloudflare Tunnel, or Cloudflare Mesh.

Unified Routing enabled on your account, unless you connect over Cloudflare Tunnel (Tunnel doesn't need it). New and existing accounts can upgrade through their account team.

If you connect over Cloudflare WAN or Cloudflare Mesh, configure a return route for Cloudflare’s source ranges: 100.64.0.0/12 for IPv4 and 2606:4700:cf1:5000::/64 for IPv6. Then, create a proxied A or AAAA record for the private IP and confirm that Use private network routing is enabled. Your existing WAF, cache, and bot management configuration applies to that hostname without further changes.

Then, create a proxied A or AAAA record for the private IP and confirm that Use private network routing is enabled. Your existing WAF, cache, and bot management configuration applies to that hostname without further changes.

One note from the beta: if requests time out and nothing arrives at the origin, check the return route first. A missing route for Cloudflare’s source range was the most common setup failure we saw.

Once enabled, follow our developer documentation, which walks through the full setup.

What comes next

Today’s release covers public traffic reaching private origins. Next, we’re working on private-to-private traffic: users, services, and AI agents on private networks reaching applications on other private networks through Cloudflare’s application services.

Engineering work is underway, and we’re targeting a closed beta in early 2027. If you’d like to participate, talk to your account team.

The goal is to give private applications the same protections and controls as public applications. An employee opening wiki.company.internal, for example, could benefit from WAF, rate limiting, and bot management. Service-to-service traffic between clouds and data centers could use those controls too, even when neither side touches the public Internet.

For now, today’s release brings the WAF, caching, bot management, and Workers you use for public applications to private origins over connectivity you already operate.

Context: If you want to compete, you need to be multi-model. And if you want to take advantage of everything that different AI models have to offer, you need a great harness. Full Text:
If you want to compete, you need to be multi-model. And if you want to take advantage of everything that different AI models have to offer, you need a great harness. But building one that works seamlessly across multiple models and surfaces is incredibly hard. You need to solve for performance, quality, and cost. And then you have to maintain it, which is even harder.

Luckily, the GitHub engineering team built a best-in-class, truly multi-model harness, which we’ve adopted company-wide. The Microsoft Copilot harness powers Copilot Code, Copilot Studio, the GitHub Copilot app, the CLI, VS Code, and more. And today, we’re making that harness available through Microsoft Foundry. That gives developers and enterprise customers a fully managed way to build agents that reason, use tools, and complete complex, long-running tasks. You get the right model for the job without switching the harness or the rest of your tech stack. That frees up your time, energy, and resources to focus on your bottom line.

What’s a harness, and why is it hard?

If the model supplies the intelligence, the harness is everything around the model. It’s the orchestration layer that gives an agent the right instructions, context, execution environment, and controls to accomplish meaningful work. And a harness worth its salt has support for open standards like MCP and agent skills, as well as agent plugins.

This is a fast-moving space. A frontier model today might fall behind tomorrow. And building your own harness or model router to keep up can be painful and slow. Now, you can build on the same harness Microsoft and GitHub ship in our own products, and you don’t have to maintain it.

We invest in science and engineering work to continually improve and evolve the harness and ensure high-quality, efficient, and low-cost performance across a range of models and workloads. The benefits compound for us and our customers who use the harness to build and run their own agents. Improve the harness, and every surface it touches benefits.

Born in GitHub, battle-tested at enterprise scale

The Copilot harness was built by the same GitHub engineers behind new technologies like our multi-model orchestration. And those technologies are only possible because we built our own harness. Designed to be fast, token-efficient, and predictable, it was our original, high-quality harness. And it had the highest satisfaction among our most demanding audience: developers. That’s why we’re standardizing all of our Copilot experiences on the strongest foundation possible.

The harness is built to perform across model families, with 20+ frontier models plus bring your own key, so you can use the right model for the right job. Instead of doing the work to keep up with and eval new models, lean on us to intelligently route work to the right model or models based on the task.

Our harness is flexible and configurable to any type of app, agent, or service. We recently ported the harness runtime to Rust, which has resulted in industry-leading performance and reductions in both session overhead and time-to-first token. And because the Copilot harness powers surfaces across Microsoft, it’s battle-tested and proven performant at the scale of millions of users and hundreds of real-world use cases.

A unified harness lets us ship faster, learn faster, and improve Copilot over time. And because the agents you build in Foundry can run on the same harness we’ve adopted across Microsoft, our continuous harness improvements will benefit your agents, too.

Try it yourself

The SDK is available to download, or you can run the harness in the cloud, all managed by Foundry. Our platforms remain open and interoperable, so you can continue to bring in any harness and framework you want, too.

With the Copilot harness, Microsoft runs the agent loop and sandbox, with governance and optimization built in from day one. You bring the instructions, skills, tools, and model choice.

This is an important step towards our vision of a stronger system around the model that preserves choice. It represents the best of GitHub, brought to the Microsoft platform and beyond.

We’ll keep pushing the harness forward, so you can focus on what only you can build.
